title: Integrated small and long RNA sequencing reveals piRNA mediated transposon repression during human oogenesis

paper_content.abstract: The piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) are essential for controlling transposable elements (TEs) activity in germ cells, yet their expression dynamics and functions during human oogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we simultaneously profile small and long RNAs in individual human oocytes across four developmental stages. piRNAs, especially PIWIL3-associated short piRNAs, are the predominant small non-coding RNAs during human oogenesis. A marked increase in short-piRNAs coincide with a global reduction of TE expression, particularly LINE-1 and endogenous retroviruses (ERVs). In contrast, PIWIL1- and PSIWIL2-associated long piRNAs correlate with the downregulation of certain specific ERV subfamilies. Genomic analyses reveal that highly productive piRNA clusters have evolved asymmetric antisense insertion bias toward LINE-1 and ERVs, enabling TE families-specific regulation. Together, our study provides a valuable single-cell dataset of small and long RNA co-expression landscapes in developing human oocytes and reveals coordinated yet distinct roles of different PIWI/piRNA classes in TE repression during human oogenesis, with short-piRNAs acting as the primary and broad-spectrum suppressors, and long-piRNAs providing coordinated ERV-specific repression.
paper_content.introduction:
Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic elements that are capable of invading and propagating within host genomes. While TE activity has played a major role in shaping genome evolution, their mobilization also poses a threat to genomic integrity by inducing DNA double-strand breaks and facilitating illegitimate recombination1, 2. Based on their mobilization mechanisms, TEs are categorized into two major classes3, 4. Class I elements, or retrotransposons, mobilize via an RNA intermediate and include both long terminal repeat (LTR) and non-LTR retrotransposons. LTR retrotransposons primarily consist of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) and ERV-derived solo LTR elements. Non-LTR retrotransposons comprise long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs) such as L1, CR1, and L2; short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) including SINE1/7SL, SINE2/tR NA, and SINE3/5S rRNA; and a composite element SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA). Class II elements, or DNA transposons, mobilize via a DNA intermediate. Although the vast majority of TEs, all DNA transposons included, are extinct, several retrotransposon families remain active in the human population5. These active elements can mobilize autonomously or rely on trans-acting factors encoded by other autonomous elements. Notably, subfamilies such as L1PA1, SVA, and AluY exhibit insertional polymorphisms among human individuals, reflecting ongoing transpositional activity6, 7. Among ERVs, HERV-K is the only lineage known to exhibit polymorphic insertions in modern humans8, 9. Additional support for their ongoing activity comes from somatic insertions observed in neuronal and cancer cells10-15, indicating their potential to mobilize post-zygotically and contribute to somatic mosaicism.

While TE repression is effectively maintained in somatic cells, genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming during primordial germ cell formation erases most DNA methylation marks, creating a vulnerable window for TE activation16-18. In females, this epigenetic state persists until the initiation of follicle growth19. Unchecked TE activity during this critical period can lead to genomic instability, meiotic arrest, and infertility20, 21. The piRNA pathway is a major defense mechanism against TE activity in the germline. PIWI proteins, a subfamily of ARGONAUTE, associate with piRNAs to mediate TE suppression via both post-transcriptional cleavage and epigenetic silencing22-31. In Drosophila and zebrafish, disruption of PIWI proteins leads to sterility in both males and females due to uncontrolled TE activity22, 32-36. In mice, the loss of Piwil1 (Miwi), Piwil2 (Mili), or Piwil4 (Miwi2) results in TE dysregulation and male infertility, whereas female oogenesis remains largely unaffected29, 32, 37, 38. Recent transcriptomic analyses of mammalian oocytes have revealed substantial variability in small RNA composition across species39. Interestingly, the Piwil3 gene is absent from the mouse genome and mouse oocytes primarily express endo-siRNAs rather than piRNAs, which are processed by a unique Dicer isoform (DicerO) and functionally substitute for piRNAs in TE suppression40. In contrast, human and most other mammalian oocytes predominantly express PIWIL3-associated short piRNAs (short-piRNAs), which account for most of the small RNAs in these cells39, 41, 42. Functional studies using golden hamsters as a model have demonstrated that loss of the piRNA pathway compromises oocyte competence and leads to early embryonic arrest43-45. Additionally, knockout studies of individual PIWI proteins suggest their non-redundant roles in TE suppression and gametogenesis46.

However, the temporal dynamics of piRNAs expression during human oogenesis and the functional relationship between distinct piRNA populations and TE regulation remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we profiled both small and long RNA transcriptomes in individual human oocytes across four key developmental stages. Our analyses reveal a global repression of TEs following the primary follicle stage, with short-piRNAs serving as the predominant and broad suppressors and long-piRNAs providing coordinated, ERV-specific repression. These findings highlight the distinct yet coordinated roles of piRNA populations in TE silencing and provide new insights into the regulatory landscape of human oocyte development.
paper_content.results:
Profiling small and long RNAs in developing human oocytes
A total of 30 human oocytes spanning four developmental stages, primordial follicle (PrF), primary follicle (PF), germinal vesicle (GV), and metaphase II (MII), were collected. Small and long RNA transcriptomes were simultaneously profiled at the single-oocyte level using our previously established protocol39, 43, 46 (Fig. 1a, Materials and Methods). To ensure high data quality for downstream analysis, we applied stringent quality-control criteria to both the small RNA and long RNA datasets. For small RNA data, we removed samples with a useful read rate below 60% after 3’ adaptor trimming and short-read filtering, a mapped read rate below 40%, or rRNA/tRNA-derived reads exceeding 30%. For long RNA data, we excluded samples with a mapped read rate below 80%, mitochondrial-derived reads exceeding 10%, or rRNA-derived reads exceeding 10%. Following quality control filtering, 23 oocytes were retained for further analyses, comprising 5 PrF, 9 PF, 4 GV, and 5 MII stage oocytes (Supplementary Data 1). On average, 5.88 million raw reads per small RNA library and 7.66 million reads per long RNA library were obtained (Supplementary Data 2). Among these retained oocytes, an average of 87.88% of small RNA-seq reads were deemed usable, with a genome mapping rate of 71.17%. Long RNA-seq libraries showed mapping rates ranging from 87.84% to 95.38%. Across all oocytes, we detected an average of 170 miRNAs, 113,861 piRNAs, and 16,145 genes (Supplementary Data 2).

Global downregulation of TEs during human oogenesis
Unsupervised principal component analysis (PCA) of protein-coding genes expression successfully segregated oocytes into four clusters, each corresponding to a different developmental stage (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 3). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of stage-specific feature genes (558 for PrF, 570 for PF, 356 for GV, and 738 for MII) revealed key biological processes associated with each stage (Supplementary Fig. 1). Genes related to RNA and protein biosynthesis were significantly overrepresented in PrF and PF stages, while pathways involved in mitotic cell cycle regulation and nuclear division were enriched in GV and MII stages, reflecting ongoing oocyte growth and maturation47.

To assess TE expression dynamics during oogenesis, we mapped long RNA-seq reads to representative human TE sequences. PCA of TE expression revealed that PrF and PF oocytes clustered together, whereas GV and MII oocytes formed separate groups (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Data 4). A progressive decline in TE-derived transcript levels was observed across developmental stages, with a marked reduction occurring after the PF stage (Fig. 1d). Specifically, 56 TE subfamilies were significantly downregulated between the PF and GV stages, while 12 subfamilies were upregulated (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Data 5). From the GV to MII stages, most TE subfamilies exhibited reductions in expression, although this reduction was less pronounced compared to the PF-to-GV transition (Fig. 1e, f).

L1 experienced the most substantial repression during oocyte development, with an average 35-fold reduction from the PrF to MII stages (Fig. 1f, g). Within the L1 clade, the primate-specific L1PA subfamily displayed the strongest downregulation, particularly L1PA2, which underwent a dramatic 129-fold downregulation (Fig. 1f). Approximately two-thirds of ERV subfamilies followed similar patterns to L1, showing progressive downregulation throughout oogenesis (Fig. 1f). For instance, HERV-L, a human specific ERV, exhibited the most substantial repression with an overall 89-fold decrease, followed by HERV-K, which demonstrated a 30-fold reduction from PrF to MII.

Despite the general trend of TE repression, approximately one-third of ERV subfamilies exhibited increasing expression from the PrF to GV stages, with eight subfamilies showing overall upregulation across oocyte development (Fig. 1f). Among these, HERVS71 exhibited the most notable increase, with a 3.4-fold upregulation. In comparison to robust silencing observed for L1 and most ERVs, Alu and SVA elements underwent relatively moderate repression, with fold changes of 4.7 and 5.4 from PrF to MII stage, respectively. Collectively, these findings indicate a hierarchical repression pattern during human oogenesis, where L1 and the majority of ERVs undergo extensive silencing, while certain ERVs, Alu and SVA elements remain relatively resilient.

piRNAs are the predominant sncRNAs during human oogenesis
Analyses of small RNA composition demonstrated that piRNAs were the most abundant sncRNAs species, accounting for 80.51% of total sncRNAs at the PrF stage and increasing to 84.19% at MII (Fig. 2a). PCA of piRNA expression profiles effectively distinguished PrF and PF oocytes, while GV and MII stages exhibited highly similar expression patterns (Fig. 2b). Among the PIWI genes, PIWIL3 was the most abundantly expressed, while PIWIL1 and PIWIL2 exhibited relatively lower expression levels, and PIWIL4 was nearly undetectable (Fig. 2c). PIWIL3 immunoprecipitation from PrF- and PF-stage oocytes, coupled with small RNA sequencing, confirmed that short-piRNAs (17–24 nt) are specifically associated with PIWIL3 (Fig. 2d). Oxidation assays further showed that these short-piRNAs lack 2′-O-methylation at the 3′ ends, as their signals were largely eliminated following oxidation (Fig. 2e). In contrast, long-piRNAs (25-35 nt), likely associated with PIWIL1 and/or PIWIL2, were resistant to oxidation (Fig. 2e), indicating 3’ terminal 2’-O-methylation. These biochemical characteristics of short- and long-piRNAs are consistent with observations in human GV and MII oocytes39, 41. The proportion of short-piRNAs increased from 44.88% at PrF to 73.21% at GV, remaining at 71.28% at MII (Fig. 2a), suggesting a predominant role of short-piRNAs in human oocyte compared to long-piRNAs. Genomic coordinate analysis showed that short- and long-piRNAs were far more likely to share 5’ ends than 3’ ends across all stages (PrF: 0.51 vs. 0.02; PF: 0.68 vs. 0.01; GV: 0.66 vs. 0.01; MII: 0.63 vs. 0.01) (Supplementary Fig. 2), suggesting that both populations are derived from the same 5’-cleaved precursors, consistent with findings in golden hamster43.

To investigate whether phased piRNA biogenesis occurs during human oocyte development, we quantified the 3′-to-5′ and 5′-to-5′ distances between piRNA ends mapped to the same genomic strand and evaluated phasing enrichment using Z-scores48. To validate this analytical strategy, we reanalyzed previously published Tdrkh⁺/⁻ and Tdrkh⁻/⁻ mouse testis datasets, in which robust piRNA phasing has been reported49. As expected, we observed a strong 1-nt peak in the 3′-to-5′ distance distribution, broad enrichment at ~30–40 nt in the 5′-to-5′ distance distribution, and a pronounced 5′-terminal uridine (1U) bias in downstream phased piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 3a-d). Applying the same analytical framework to piRNAs derived from developing human oocytes revealed significant enrichment at a 1-nt separation in the 3′-to-5′ distance distribution (Z-scores 3.6–6.8) (Supplementary Fig. 3e), indicative of phased piRNA processing. Notably, short-piRNAs displayed stronger phasing signals than long-piRNAs. Downstream phased piRNAs showed a pronounced 5′-terminal U bias, particularly among short-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 3g-h), consistent with canonical phased piRNA signatures in mammals. However, no prominent peaks were observed in the 5′-to-5′ distance distribution (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Unexpectedly, enrichment at a 0-nt separation exceeded that at a 1-nt separation in the 3′-to-5′ distance distribution (Supplementary Fig. 3e), indicating frequent 1-nt overlaps between adjacent piRNAs. These 1-nt-overlapping downstream piRNAs retained a strong 5′-terminal U bias, whereas their upstream counterparts exhibited marked enrichment for 3’-terminal uridine (Supplementary Fig. 3i, j). This distinctive overlap pattern may result from frequent 3′ non-templated uridylation of piRNAs, a possibility that warrants further investigation through perturbation of enzymes involved in piRNA 3′-end tailing.

Unlike in mouse oocytes, endo-siRNAs were undetectable at any sequenced developmental stage of human oocytes, aligning with observations in golden hamsters and other mammals39, 43-45 (Fig. 2a). miRNAs, which constituted 0.34% of total sncRNAs in the PrF stage oocytes, exhibited a modest increase after the GV stage (Fig. 2a). miRNA expression profiles grouped the oocytes into two distinct clusters: PrF/PF and GV/MII (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Data 6). Feature analyses identified 11 miRNAs highly enriched in PrF and PF stage oocytes, while 58 miRNAs were upregulated at GV/MII stage oocytes (Fig. 3c). Reactome pathway enrichment analysis revealed that these miRNAs are involved in pathways related to RUNX2, ALK, and TP53, as well as growth factor receptor signaling, second messenger systems, and MAPK signaling (Fig. 3d). Among the ARGONAUTE (AGO) genes, AGO2 was predominantly expressed, with expression progressively increasing during human oogenesis, while AGO1 and AGO3 exhibited consistently low expression (Fig. 3b). AGO4 was barely detectable in any analyzed stage, in line with its established distinctive role in spermatogenesis50, 51. Although miRNAs were expressed at lower levels in oocytes than in somatic cells, their stage-specific expression, the progressive upregulation of AGO2, and enrichment of their targets in critical signaling pathways suggest that miRNAs may contribute to oocyte development and warrant further investigation. Overall, these findings underscore the dominant role of piRNAs, particularly short-piRNAs, in human oogenesis.

Conserved TE preference of short- and long-piRNAs
To explore the potential contribution of piRNAs to global TE downregulation, we mapped short- and long-piRNAs separately to representative human TE sequences on both sense and antisense strands. Remarkably, approximately 80% of long-piRNAs were associated with ERVs across all developmental stages, compared to around 50% of short-piRNAs (Fig. 4a, b). This preference was largely driven by antisense-aligned long-piRNAs. At the PrF stage, 80.64% of all TE-aligned long-piRNAs were antisense ERV-related, compared to only 5.86% for sense ERV-related, resulting in an antisense-to-sense ratio greater than 13. Although this ratio decreased as development progressed, the bias toward antisense persisted, with a 4.7-fold preference at the MII stage. In contrast, short-piRNAs exhibited a broader association across various TE superfamilies, accompanied by a more balanced antisense-to-sense ratio, generally ranging between 2 to 3 throughout oogenesis (Fig. 4a, b).

Notably, the preference for ERV association among long-piRNAs was conserved across species. In cynomolgus monkey (Macaca fascicularis) and golden hamster MII oocytes, 72.49% and 69.69% of long-piRNAs, respectively, were ERV-related, compared to 53.21% and 43.87% of short-piRNAs (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). In addition, the antisense-to-sense strand ratio for ERV-related long-piRNAs exceeded 10 in golden hamster oocytes, whereas there was almost no bias for ERV-related short-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Collectively, these results suggest that TE-related antisense long-piRNAs exhibit a conserved, preferential targeting of ERVs across species, indicating their specialized role in ERV repression. In contrast, TE-related antisense short-piRNAs exhibit broader TE targeting, likely reflecting their more generalized silencing function across multiple TE families.

The widespread role of short-piRNAs in TE downregulation
Analyses of TE-aligned short-piRNA expression revealed three distinct groups corresponding to the PrF, PF, and GV/MII stages (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Data 4). A marked upregulation of short-piRNA was observed from PrF to GV stages during oogenesis (Fig. 5b, c). From PrF to PF, 162 TE subfamilies exhibited significant increases in short-piRNAs expression, nearly twice as many as those showing downregulation. From PF to GV, 130 TE subfamilies showed upregulated short-piRNAs, while only seven were downregulated (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Data 7). Notably, the upregulation of short-piRNAs preceded the onset of substantial TE reduction, which was primarily initiated after the PF stage (Fig. 1d, e), indicating a temporal delay in the repressive effects of short-piRNAs on TE activity at the mRNA levels.

Among TE superfamilies, L1-related short-piRNAs exhibited the most pronounced upregulation throughout oogenesis, aligning with L1 being the most substantially downregulated TE superfamily (Fig. 5d, Fig. 1g, and Supplementary Fig. 5a). Following L1, ERV-related short-piRNAs displayed the second most prominent upregulation, although considerable heterogeneity was detected across different ERV subfamilies, mirroring the varied repression patterns observed in these elements. In addition, Alu- and SVA-related short-piRNAs showed relatively modest increases, mainly during the PF-to-GV transition, consistent with their comparatively moderate downregulation (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 5a). A robust inverse correlation between TE downregulation levels and the upregulation levels of corresponding short-piRNAs further supports the contribution of short-piRNAs to global TE repression (Fig. 5e).

The Ping-Pong amplification mechanism is essential for the post-transcriptional TE repression via PIWI/piRNA-mediated cleavage of target RNAs, generating complementary piRNA pairs with a characteristic 10-nt overlap at their 5’ ends52, 53. This process also exhibits an uracil (U) preference at the first nucleotide (1U) of antisense piRNAs, and an adenine (A) bias at the tenth nucleotide (10A) in sense. Indeed, high 1U and 10A preferences were observed in retrotransposons-associated piRNAs (sense strand 1U: 89.14%, 10A: 62.85%; antisense strand 1U: 87.86%, 10A: 44.31%, Supplementary Fig. 5b, c). Among TE superfamilies, Alu- and SVA-associated piRNAs exhibited the strongest Ping-Pong signatures, followed by moderate activity for L1 and weak activity for ERV (Supplementary Fig. 5d). We next examined Ping-Pong activity at the level of individual TE subfamilies. Specifically, short-piRNAs related to most of the L1, Alu, and SVA subfamilies showed strong Ping-Pong signatures (Fig. 5f), with the intensity of these signatures correlating with their progressive downregulation throughout oocyte development. However, this signature was less prevalent among ERV-related short-piRNAs, with notable exceptions such as THER1A and THER1B. Notably, approximately two-thirds of L1 subfamilies exhibited strong Ping-Pong activity (Group A) and consistently showed higher 1U and 10A proportions, greater antisense and sense piRNA abundance, and elevated transcript levels compared with those with low signals (Group B) (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). Interestingly, genomic analysis of the top 20 piRNA clusters revealed that Group B L1 subfamilies carried more antisense insertions than Group A, while sense insertions were comparable (Supplementary Fig. 6c). Given the lower abundance of both antisense and sense piRNAs for Group B, these results suggest that primary processing and PIWI loading preferentially enhance piRNA biogenesis from Group A L1 subfamilies. These findings indicate that weak Ping-Pong activity in certain L1 subfamilies likely reflects their lower transcript abundance and inefficient primary piRNA processing. Collectively, these observations suggest that the PIWIL3-mediated Ping-Pong pathway may contribute to the extensive regulatory influence of short-piRNAs on TE repression during human oogenesis.

Although the majority of piRNAs mapped to various TE families, a notable minority (5-10%) originated from coding or other exonic non-TE genomic regions (Supplementary Fig. 5b, c). Unlike TE-related piRNAs, these piRNAs lacked the characteristic 10A bias (Supplementary Fig. 5c), suggesting they may participate in gene regulation through Ping-Pong–independent mechanisms.

Long piRNAs play a collaborative role in ERV repression
TE-aligned long-piRNA expression segregated oocytes into three distinct groups: PrF, PF, and GV/MII stages (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 4). However, long-piRNAs were less effective than short-piRNAs in distinguishing PrF from PF stage oocytes. Unlike the widespread upregulation of short-piRNAs during oogenesis, TE-aligned long-piRNAs showed a declining trend in expression (Fig. 6b, c). Differential expression analysis revealed a substantial decrease in TE-aligned long-piRNAs between the PF and GV stages, with 58 TE subfamilies exhibiting significant downregulation of their corresponding long-piRNAs, compared to 13 subfamilies that were upregulated (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Data 8). Despite the overall decline, 18 ERV subfamilies and two derivative LTR elements exhibited significant upregulation of their associated long-piRNAs, aligning with the preferential ERV targeting by long-piRNAs (Fig. 6d and Fig. 4a, b).

The Ping-Pong signature was either undetectable or substantially reduced for most TE-aligned long-piRNAs comparing with short-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 7a), including those ERVs or solo LTRs with upregulated long-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Analysis of TE-related piRNAs using the adult human ovary dataset from a previous study54 further confirmed that long-piRNAs exhibited weaker Ping-Pong signatures than short-piRNAs for SVA and Alu elements, whereas L1 and ERV showed very low or undetectable Ping-Pong signatures (Supplementary Fig. 8).

To examine the cooperative contributions of short- and long-piRNAs to TE repression during human oogenesis, we assessed the overlap among TEs with significantly altered mRNA levels (upregulated or downregulated), TEs with upregulated short-piRNAs, and those with upregulated long-piRNAs (Fig. 6e). Of the 96 downregulated TE subfamilies, 61.46% (59 out of 96) were associated with either upregulated short- or long-piRNAs. Among these, 93.22% (55 out of 59) were associated with upregulated short-piRNAs, while 20.34% (12 out of 59), most of which belonged to ERV subfamilies, were linked to upregulated long-piRNAs. L1HS and L1PA2 represent TE subfamilies that are primarily regulated by short-piRNAs with downregulation levels correlated inversely with a gradual increase in corresponding antisense and sense short-piRNAs and accompanied by prominent Ping-Pong signatures (Fig. 6f, Supplementary Fig. 9, and Supplementary Fig.10). For HERV-K, only sense short-piRNAs were markedly increased, and this increase was significantly correlated with reduced HERV-K transcript levels (Supplementary Fig. 9d and Supplementary Fig. 10d). Among the TE subfamilies associated with long-piRNAs, 66.67% (8 out of 12) also showed upregulation of short-piRNAs, suggesting a coordinated role for both piRNA classes in repressing these elements. HERV-L, one of the most strongly downregulated ERV subfamilies, showed an inverse correlation with both antisense and sense short- and long-piRNAs during oocyte development (Fig. 6g and Supplementary Fig. 10c), accompanied by a weak but detectable Ping-Pong signature. All these observations suggest a dominant role for short-piRNAs in broad TE repression, with long-piRNAs contributing to ERV-specific repression.

In addition, we identified eight TE subfamilies, including HERVS71, LTR25, MER11D, LTR1C1, LTR17, LTR6B, LTR14A, and LTR3B, that remained transcriptionally active during human oogenesis (Fig. 1f and Fig. 6e). Compared with TE subfamilies that were downregulated, these upregulated TE subfamilies showed higher transcript abundance but produced markedly fewer corresponding antisense and sense short- and long-piRNAs, accompanied by weaker Ping-Pong signatures and reduced 1U and 10A biases (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Genomic distribution analyses within the top 20 piRNA clusters further revealed substantially fewer antisense insertions for these upregulated TE subfamilies relative to downregulated TE subfamilies, consistent with their reduced antisense piRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 11b). Notably, seven of these elements, with the exception of LTR1C1, are specific to the human genome. The limited or absent repression of these evolutionarily younger elements may reflect a lag in the adaptation of the piRNA/PIWI system to those recently emerged transposon threats.

Highly productive piRNA clusters show antisense bias
Primary piRNA biogenesis is tightly associated with specific genomic loci across various species25, 53, 55. To determine the genomic origins of piRNAs expressed during human oogenesis, we employed a proximity-based clustering strategy adapted from the piClust algorithm56. Using a threshold of at least four uniquely mapped piRNAs within a 2.5-kilobase (kb) window and merging overlapping regions, we identified 14,603 piRNA-generating clusters. Remarkably, the top 20 most highly expressed clusters accounted for 91.72 % of all uniquely mapped piRNAs (Fig. 7a, b, and Supplementary Data 9) and generated both short- and long-piRNAs, with short-piRNA production generally increasing as oogenesis progressed (Fig. 7c). These clusters displayed dynamic expression patterns during oocyte development, with their contributions to TE-related piRNA population varying by stage (Fig. 7a, b, and Supplementary Data 9). For example, the cluster chr4:78106722–78396420|+ ranked second for L1 antisense short-piRNA generation at the PrF and PF stages, but became the predominant source at the GV/MII stages. Similarly, the cluster chr12:114437233–114625671|− produced the second-largest number of ERV antisense short piRNAs at the PrF stage and emerged as the primary contributor after the PF stage. Notably, only two pairs of bidirectionally transcribed clusters were identified among the top 20 piRNA clusters (Supplementary Fig. 12), and expanding the analysis to the top 100 clusters revealed two additional pairs. This indicates that, in contrast to pachytene piRNAs in mouse testis57, only a small fraction of human oocyte piRNA clusters arises from bidirectionally transcribed loci, consistent with observations in golden hamster oocytes58.

TE enrichment analysis revealed a strong bias toward ERV fragments within the top 10 clusters, particularly for the antisense strand, when compared to genomic background regions (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 13 and Supplementary Data 10). This asymmetric insertion pattern facilitated the preferential generation of antisense-aligned piRNAs targeting ERVs (Supplementary Fig. 13b). This phenomenon is reminiscent of the flamenco/COM locus in Drosophila, which generates antisense piRNAs to silence gypsy, Idefix, and ZAM elements53, 59, 60. Interestingly, although L1 elements did not show a pronounced difference in antisense versus sense insertion frequencies, the top 10 piRNA clusters still produced markedly more antisense than sense piRNAs (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 13a). This suggests selective primary processing, in which L1 antisense piRNAs may be preferentially generated or more efficiently loaded onto PIWI proteins. In contrast, Alu elements were not enriched in these top clusters compared to genomic background regions (Fig. 7d and Supplementary Fig. 13c), consistent with the relatively low production of Alu-derived piRNAs and their modest repression during oocyte development.

The most productive piRNA cluster, spanning approximately 320 kb between WDR1 and ZFN518B on chromosome 4, contributed 34.05% of all uniquely mapped piRNAs. This unidirectionally transcribed cluster contained abundant antisense insertions of L1 and ERVs (Fig. 8a) and generated numerous short- and long-piRNAs targeting these elements (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b). Similarly, the second most productive cluster, also on chromosome 4 (~300 kb between CCNG2 and CXCL13), contributed 15.41% of uniquely mapped piRNAs and displayed a comparable enrichment for antisense insertion of L1 and ERVs (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b and Supplementary Fig. 14a). By contrast, the third most productive cluster featured minimal L1 context but was enriched for ERVs, producing predominantly antisense piRNAs targeting ERVs (Supplementary Fig. 13a, b and Supplementary Fig. 14b). This suggests that this cluster primarily functions as a specialized regulator of ERVs, distinct from the broader TE repression roles observed in the top two clusters.

SVA, a relatively young TE element with approximately 4,000 annotated copies in the human genome, was represented by antisense insertions in one of the top 20 clusters. This insertion was accompanied by the production of SVA-targeting antisense piRNAs (Fig. 7d, Fig. 8b, and Supplementary Fig. 13d), suggesting that this cluster may serve as a SVA suppressor. Conversely, L2 elements, which are largely inactive in the human genome, were absent from the top clusters (Supplementary Fig. 13e). These patterns suggest that evolutionary pressures preferentially shape the composition and activity of piRNA clusters based on the functional relevance and activity of specific TE families. Taken together, these findings indicate the unique evolutionary dynamics of human piRNA clusters and their adaptive specialization in repressing diverse and evolving TE populations during oocyte development.
paper_content.methods:
Ethics statement
The study was approved by the Reproductive Study Ethics Committee of Shanghai Zhongshan Hospital (approval number: B2018-244). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to oocyte donation, and no compensation was provided, following clinical protocols of the Department of Assisted Reproduction at Zhongshan Hospital, affiliated with Fudan University, Shanghai, China. All human participants were female, as the study focused on oocyte development. No sex or gender analysis was conducted because it was not applicable. The original tissue samples and oocytes were fully consumed and are not available for further use.

Human oocyte collection
Human follicles were isolated from fresh ovarian cortex obtained from patients undergoing ovarian cyst or cystic teratoma resection, following previously described procedures78. Briefly, ovarian cortical tissues were fragmented into pieces measuring 30–600 μm and digested with 1 mg/mL collagenase type IA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 8 IU/mL DNase I (Sigma-Aldrich) in 10 mL of M199 medium (Gibco) at 37°C for 30 minutes with gentle agitation. Follicles were subsequently isolated and evaluated under a stereomicroscope (Nikon SMZ 1000), and their diameters were measured using an inverted microscope (Nikon Ti2).

Ovarian stimulation and oocyte collection were performed as previously described41, 78. GV oocytes were collected following stimulation. MII stage oocytes were obtained after overnight incubation to facilitate maturation, characterized by the presence of a distinct first polar body under microscope observation.

For all oocytes at all developmental stages, granulosa cells were removed via incubation with 1 mg/mL hyaluronidase. The zona pellucida was eliminated using Acidic Tyrode's Solution (Millipore), yielding denuded oocytes, which were then washed and transferred to PCR tubes containing 4 μL of cell lysis buffer (0.2% Triton X-100, Sigma; 1 U/μL RiboLock RNase inhibitor, Thermo Fisher). The oocytes were stored at -80°C until further processing.

Single-oocyte small-RNA library construction
Single-oocyte small-RNA libraries were constructed as previously described43. Briefly, lysates from the single oocyte were incubated at 72 °C for 3 minutes to release and unfold the small RNAs. After 3’ adapter ligation, 5 U of lambda exonuclease and 25 U of 5′ deadenylates were used to remove the excess 3’ adapter. Subsequently, the 5′ adapter was ligated, followed by reverse transcription and pre-amplification. For final amplification, 1 μL of the pre-amplified product was used as a template. Libraries were size-selected by electrophoresis on a 6% polyacrylamide gel, and 130–160 bp DNA fragments were extracted to recover small RNA libraries. Sequencing was performed on the HiSeq X Ten platform (Illumina) using 2 × 150 bp reads. Oligonucleotide sequences are provided in the Supplementary Data 11.

Single-cell mRNA library construction
Single-oocyte mRNA was captured and amplified using Smart-seq2, as previously described43, 79. In brief, single oocytes or embryos were incubated at 72°C for 3 min to release the RNAs. For every single oocyte or embryo, 0.125 μL 1/100,000 dilution of the ERCC RNA Spike-In Mix (Invitrogen, Cat# 4456740) was used. Following reverse transcription and PCR pre-amplification, cDNA libraries were purified by Agencourt Ampure XP beads (0.8:1 ratio) (Beckman Coulter, Cat#A63881). 2 ng of purified cDNA was subjected to a tagmentation reaction with Tn5 transposase80. Sequencing was carried out on the Illumina HiSeq X Ten platform with 2x150 bp reads. Oligonucleotide sequences are provided in the Supplementary Data 11.

Immunoprecipitation
Five PrF or PF oocytes were lysed on ice for 10 min in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5% NP-40, 0.5 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1 U μL−1 RNase Inhibitor (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 0.4 U μL–1 proteinase inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich). Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were washed once with lysis buffer and incubated with 1 μg of homemade anti-PIWIL3 or rabbit IgG at room temperature for 40 min. The oocyte lysates were mixed with antibody-coupled beads and rotated gently at 4 °C for 5 h. The beads were then washed three times with lysis buffer and once with PBS, and RNA was eluted from the beads by adding 4 μL of nuclease-free water and followed by incubation at 72 °C for 5 min with gentle agitation. The supernatant containing the RNA was collected using a magnetic holder and used for small RNA library construction.

NaIO oxidation of oocyte RNAs
Total RNAs were extracted from five PrF and PF oocytes using TRIzol Reagent (Ambion) supplemented with 8.14 × 10−3 pmol of spike-in oligos. RNA pellets were dissolved in 4 μL of water. Half of the RNA was reserved as a non-oxidation control, and the remaining half was treated with an oxidation reaction mixture containing 1.5 μL of 100 mM NaIO4 (Sigma-Aldrich), 2 μL of 5× borate buffer (150 mM borax, 150 mM boric acid, pH 8.6), and 4.5 μL of water. The reaction mixtures were incubated in the dark at room temperature for 30 min, followed by RNA precipitation with 600 μL of 100% ethanol, 25 μg of linear acrylamide, and 30 μL of 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.2). Samples were incubated at −30 °C for 30 min, centrifuged, and washed twice with 75% ethanol. The RNA pellets were dissolved in 2 μL of water and used for small RNA library preparation.

Data processing of small RNA-seq and long RNA-seq
For small RNA-seq, raw read1 sequences were processed using the fastx_toolkit (v.0.0.14) for quality filtering and adapter trimming. Reads lacking the 3’ adapter sequence or shorter than 17 bp post-trimming were discarded. Reads of 17-40 bp were mapped to the human genome (hg19) using Bowtie (v.1.2) with parameters --k=100 --v=0.

For long RNA-seq, raw pair-end reads were processed using TrimGalore (v.0.5.0) for adapter trimming and quality filtering. The remaining reads were mapped to the human genome (hg19) and representative TE sequences using STAR (v2.7.1a) with parameters --winAnchorMultimapNmax 10000 --outFilterMultimapNmax 10000. Gene abundance was quantified using RSEM (v.1.2.31) with default settings.

For multiply mapped piRNAs or long RNA-seq reads, each read was assigned to all possible mapped loci and categorized by TE superfamily in the following order: LINE/L1 → SINE/Alu → LTR/ERV → LTR/others → SVA → others. If a read or piRNA species mapped to multiple TE subfamilies within the same superfamily, it was counted in each TE family. When summarizing results at the superfamily level (e.g., LINE/L1), each piRNA or read was counted only once. This uniform assignment strategy was applied to all TE-related analyses, including TE transcript abundance, TE-associated short and long piRNAs, and strand-specific subsets, to ensure consistent quantification and accurate cross-dataset comparison.

Categorization of small non-coding RNA
Mapped small RNA-seq reads were further aligned to annotations of small non-coding RNAs in the following order: pre-miRNAs, tRNAs, rRNAs, snoRNAs, and snRNAs, using Bowtie (v.1.2) with parameters --a --v=0 --norc. Reads that precisely matched the 5’ start site of miRNAs and 3’ ends with less than 3 bp deletions or additions derived from pre-miRNAs were considered for miRNA quantification.

Unassigned sequences that were not categorized as pre-miRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snoRNA, or snRNA, with lengths ranging from 17–40 nt, were identified as piRNA clusters using a modified piClust with MinReads=4 and Eps=2500 bp. Overlapping clusters were merged using mergeBed from bedtools (v.2.30.0). Reads mapping within these clusters were defined as piRNA candidates. piRNA candidates were subsequently aligned to representative TE sequences using Bowtie with the parameters --a --v = 2. Based on alignment orientation, piRNAs were classified as TE-aligned antisense piRNAs (mapping to the opposite strand of TEs) or TE-aligned sense piRNAs (mapping to the same strand of TEs). Reads were further categorized by TE superfamily in the following order: LINE/L1, SINE/Alu, LTR/ERVs, LTR/others, SVA, and others. If a read mapped to multiple TE subfamilies within a superfamily, it was counted simultaneously for each subfamily.

Cell Clustering and Feature Gene Analysis
Cell clustering based on gene, TE, miRNA, and piRNA expression levels was performed using principal component analysis in Seurat (v.2.3.4). Feature genes for each stage were identified using FindAllMarkers from Seurat, and enriched pathways were analyzed using Gene Ontology website.

Differential Expression Analysis
Differential expression of TEs and their aligned piRNAs was analyzed using DESeq2, with thresholds of fold change ≥ 1.50 or ≤0.67 and p-value ≤0.05. TEs or aligned piRNAs with average expression levels below 100 RPM across all samples were excluded from this analysis.

Identification of Ping-Pong signature
Ping-Pong signatures were detected by calculating the Z score of 10-nucleotide overlaps of piRNAs from opposite strands. A Z score > 1.96 was considered significant57 (p < 0.05).

Sources of Annotations
Human (hg19) and cynomolgus monkey (Macaca fascicularis, MacFas5) genome sequences were obtained from the UCSC Genome Browser, while the golden hamster genome (MesAur1.0) was retrieved from Ensembl. For human and cynomolgus monkey, the representative sequences of TEs were retrieved from RepBase, and genomic TE annotations were sourced from UCSC. For the hamster, TE sequences and annotations were obtained following previously published protocols43, 46. Gene annotations for hg19 were sourced from GENCODE (version 19). Functional RNA annotations for human were obtained from miRBase (pre-miRNAs and miRNAs), Genomic tRNA Database (tRNAs), NCBI GenBank (18S and 28S rRNAs), and Ensembl (5S and 5.8S rRNAs, snoRNA and snRNAs).

Statistics and Reproducibility
No formal statistical method was used to predetermine the sample size. Sample sizes were determined based on prior studies to ensure reliable measurement of experimental parameters according to field standards39, 41, 43-45, 81. Samples were randomly allocated, and blinding was implemented during library construction. A total of 7 (PrF), 12 (PF), 4 (GV), and 7 (MII) oocytes were collected at each stage, of which 5 (PrF), 9 (PF), 4 (GV), and 5 (MII) were retained after quality filtering and included in downstream analyses. Data analyses were conducted using R version 3.6.3. Results are presented as mean ± standard deviation (s.d.), with statistical tests and p values provided in figure legends.

Data Availability
The sequencing data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI GEO database under accession number GSE296363 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE296363]. Publicly available datasets used in this study include small-RNA sequencing data for golden hamsters from GSE16952843 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE169528] and cynomolgus monkey MII oocytes from GSE9521841 [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE95218].

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The Piwi-piRNA pathway is an evolutionarily conserved germline specific repressor of transposable elements (TEs). In their manuscript "Integrated small and long RNA sequencing in single oocytes reveals piRNA-mediated transposon repression during human oogenesis," Zhang et al., extending their previous analysis of human piRNAs (Ref 41), characterized piRNAs during human oocyte maturation at single cell levels. The results suggest a model in which short-piRNAs (17-24nt) act as the primary and broad-spectrum TE suppressors and long-piRNAs (25-35nt) provide coordinated endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-specific silencing. Overall, the results are extensively presented and the main conclusions are supported by the data. Studies of this sort are good references and resources for further comparisons, However, once the points below are addressed I feel that the manuscript may be suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
Below we list several areas that in our opinion warrant improvement. We also suggest additional analyses that, if fruitful, may elevate the biological significance of the study.
1. By definition, piRNAs are small RNAs loaded onto PIWI proteins. They previously examined PIWI-associated small RNAs (Ref 41). However, in this study, they sequenced total small RNAs. How do they know “short-piRNAs” are indeed piRNAs and associated with PIWIL3? How many of piRNAs identified here are identical to those identified in the previous study (Ref 41)? Do they exhibit no characteristics of endo-siRNAs with 2nt overhangs and complete complementarity?
2. Figure 1f (line 136-144): The authors show that L1PA2 has undergone a 128.90-fold downregulation while HERV-L and HERV-K have exhibited a 89.43-fold and a 29.50-fold repression, respectively. The authors should show expression levels of corresponding piRNAs (just like Figure 4e). This will help the reader understand the relationship between expression levels of piRNAs and degree of TE repression.
3. Figure 1f: Some group of ERVs are upregulated during oocyte development. What might distinguish this group of TEs from other TEs which are downregulated during oocyte development. Are these TEs located in piRNA clusters identified in this study?
4. Line 166: “3’-O-methylation” should be “2’-O-methylation at the 3’ end.” The authors should describe methods used to examine the presence/absence of this modification. This reviewer cannot find methods used in Methods.
5. Figure 4f: It is peculiar that the authors do not cite the paper of Ishino et al. (NAR 49, 2700-2720, 2021) and discuss the discrepancy between the two studies. Ishino et al. conclude that most of the piRNAs expressed in oocytes are not involved in the ping-pong cycle.
6. Figure 4f: L1 subfamilies are largely divided into two subgroups in terms of the z-score of ping-pong signature (high vs low). Why? Is the low z-score due to the primary processing? Is there any peculiarity of piRNAs in this group?
7. Figure 6a-d (line 311-313): The authors claim a strong bias toward L1 and ERV fragments within the top 20 clusters. However, 11 out of the top 20 clusters show L1 antisense bias, which does not seem statistically strong. Could these data imply that piRNA clusters are differentially expressed at each stage of oocyte development? Do piRNA cluster share common promoters/transcription factor binding sites in a stage-specific manner, for example?
8. Figure 6e: How do the authors know that the piRNA cluster is unidirectionally transcribed? Are short-piRNAs produced by the ping-pong cycle derived from unidirectionally transcribed cluster transcripts?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Integrated small and long RNA sequencing in single oocytes reveals piRNA-mediated transposon repression during human oogenesis
The manuscript describes the expression, by nucleotide sequencing, of small non coding RNAs, mRNAs and transposon elements in human oocytes of 4 different developmental stages: primordial follicle, primary follicle, germinal vesicle and metaphase II. It is concluded that short piwi interacting RNAs (piRNAs) act as primary suppressors of transposon activity, while long piRNAS coordinate silencing of specific ERV transposons.
In general, the manuscript provides a nice descriptive dataset of expressed piRNA and transposon sequences at different stage of human oocytes. In that respect it is of value to the scientific community.
Functional data that demonstrate the activity of certain piRNAs, or how possible transposon activity would affect the quality of the oocyte or a possible developing embryo are lacking however. This limits the conclusions that can be drawn from the data, and as such it is merely a descriptive manuscript. There may be correlation, but there is no demonstration of a causation.
Major comments.
The analysis of piRNA, PIWI protein genes and transposon expression of human oocytes at different developmental stages is solid, well described and well presented in clear figures. The sequencing, though solid and extensive, is not novel. Similar data have been published previously eg PMID: 34340992; PMID: 33622565; PMID: 25818294; PMID: 31358756.
Functional data are lacking in the manuscript. In that sense it is descriptive, and conclusions drawn are rather speculative. Different interpretations of the data are possible, and how presence of absence of piRNAs would affect the quality and functionality of oocytes remains unknown.
Although in the introduction it is mentioned that in mice oocytes transposon activity is thought to be regulated via miRNAs and a specific Dicer isoform, crucial information here that the mouse genome does not harbour Piwil3 should be mentioned.
In the results section it is stated that 30 oocytes were collected. The value of this number is limited, as only 23 oocytes were used. The numbers is Fig1A ae misleading: PrF n=7: only 5 were used, PF n=12: only 9 were used, MII n=7: only 5 were used.
It is not clear whether the somatic cells surrounding the oocytes (granulosa and cumulus) were removed. For the GV and MII oocytes it is evident that these were removed but for the oocytes from primordial follicles this is less clear. How certain are the authors that all somatic cells were indeed removed? Indeed in figure 1a, the oocytes are presented with somatic cells present.
Fig 1c, and 2d, the colored areas are a bit misleading, just the colored dots would be more informative and realistic.
In the different violin plots such as Fig 1g, 2c, 2e, 4b, 4d,5f, 5g indications of which data sets differ statistically from others is essential.
The use of the word ‘repression’ is suggestive, or misleading, as it indicates and active mechanism. For instance in line 150 where it is stated that Alu and SVA elements underwent repression with fold changes of 4.71 and 5.36. What is the indication that these elements were repressed, rather than having reduced expression? From these data there is no indication of repression. Similar for ‘robust silencing’ in line 149. There are no experimental data indicating that the expression is actively silenced, instead of expression simply being at a lower level.
The manuscript is concentrated on indicating that piRNAs are important for reducing transposon activity. At the same time, expression of miRNAs, even at low levels, is suggested to ‘ contribute to oocyte development’ line 188. Although it is understandable that piRNAs are linked with suppression of TE activity, the data presented in this manuscript do not exclude that piRNA, similar to miRNAs, have another role besides repression of TE activity that is beneficial for acquiring oocyte developmental competence.
On the same note, expression of several TE increase during oocyte development (line 148; fig 1f). What is the proposed function of this increased expression. Could it be important for acquisition of developmental competence?
Fig 2g is difficult to read, individual lines/arrows cannot be distinguished. As such the figure is not informative.
Figure 3c, ‘ Monkey’ is a general term, it should be further specified; eg Macaca fascicularis, or whichever species was used here.
Line 267 The Ping-Pong signature was either undetectable or 267 substantially diminished for most TE-aligned long-piRNAs. How does this vibe with other publications such as PMID: 25818294?
The conclusions are too strong. For instance line 352, a role for piRAs has not been provided, but suggested. By examining piRNA and TE expression levels, it is by no means demonstrated that these affect each other. Line 352, the results do not ‘emphasize the suppressive effects of piRNAs on TE’, but instead provide a correlation between piRNAs and TEs.
Line 364-371: It should be made clear that (control of) TE activity in germ cells is different from TE activity in somatic cells.
Minor
Line 34 ‘(long-piRNAs)’ can be removed.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thorough and constructive evaluation of our manuscript. We are encouraged that the reviewer found our results comprehensive, our main conclusions well supported by the data, and our study potentially valuable as a reference for future research. We also greatly appreciate the reviewer’s recognition of the novelty of our analyses and of the biological model we propose for the roles of short- and long-piRNAs in TE regulation in human developing oocytes.
We further thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and professional suggestions, which have substantially strengthened the biological significance and overall quality of our study after incorporation. We have carefully revised the manuscript in response to all points. Below, we provide a detailed, point-by-point response, highlighting the corresponding revisions made to the text, figures, and supplementary materials where appropriate.
1. By definition, piRNAs are small RNAs loaded onto PIWI proteins. They previously examined PIWI-associated small RNAs (Ref 41). However, in this study, they sequenced total small RNAs. How do they know “short-piRNAs” are indeed piRNAs and associated with PIWIL3? How many of piRNAs identified here are identical to those identified in the previous study? Do they exhibit no characteristics of endo-siRNAs with 2nt overhangs and complete complementarity?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important points. In our previous work, we identified that ~19-nt piRNAs associate with PIWIL3 and lack 2’-O-methylation at their 3’ ends (1, 2). In the revised manuscript, we performed PIWIL3 immunoprecipitation (PIWIL3-IP) from human primordial and primary follicle oocytes, followed by sequencing of the associated small RNAs. This analysis confirmed that PIWIL3 specifically binds short-piRNAs with a size peak at 17–24 nt (Fig. 2d). Furthermore, we verified that most of short-piRNAs lack 2′-O-methylation at their 3′ ends, as their signals were largely eliminated after oxidation treatment (Fig. 2e). In contrast, long-piRNAs (25-35 nt) were resistant to oxidation (Fig. 2e), indicating 3’ terminal 2’-O-methylation. These biochemical characteristics of short- and long-piRNAs are consistent with observations in human GV and MII oocytes (1, 2). The new analyses have been incorporated into (Fig. 2d, e) and described in the corresponding Results section (Line 171-179) of the revised manuscript. The corresponding experimental details have been provided in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 528-551).
Figure 2. piRNAs are the predominant small non-coding RNAs during human oogenesis.
(d) Length distribution of PIWIL3-associated small RNAs and total small RNAs from input oocytes. The PIWIL3-bound fraction is enriched for short-piRNAs (17-24 nt), whereas input samples contain both short (17-24 nt) and long-piRNAs (25-35 nt). Approximately 2.5 oocytes were pooled per sample for the IP assay.
(e) Length profiles of small RNAs before and after oxidation treatment in PrF and PF oocytes. Short-piRNAs (17-24 nt) were largely depleted upon oxidation, whereas long-piRNAs (25-35 nt) were largely retained, confirming the absence of 2’-O-methylation in short-piRNAs and its presence in long-piRNAs. Approximately 2.5 oocytes were pooled per sample for each oxidation assay.
Next, we compared the short-piRNAs identified in this study with previously reported PIWIL3-IP and oxidation-treated libraries from human GV and MII oocytes (1, 2). We found that approximately 50% of short-piRNAs overlapped with PIWIL3-associated sequences. Consistently, short-piRNAs were more abundant in non-oxidized than in oxidized libraries (Rebuttal Figure 1).
Rebuttal Figure 1. Comparison of short-piRNAs in this study with previously reported PIWIL3-IP and oxidation-treated libraries from human GV and MII oocytes.
(a) Proportion of short-piRNAs identified in GV and MII oocytes from this study that overlap with PIWIL3-associated sequences.
(b) Comparison of short-piRNAs identified in GV and MII oocytes from this study with previously reported oxidized and non-oxidized small RNA libraries. In both (a) and (b), PIWIL3-IP, oxidation, and non-oxidation treatments were performed using pooled GV and MII oocytes (1, 2). Statistical significance was evaluated using the Wilcoxon test.
Next, we examined the sequence characteristics of these short-piRNAs. To validate the accuracy of our analytical pipeline for detecting 2-nt 3’ overhangs, we first applied it to analyze endo-siRNAs in mouse oocytes. As expected, we observed a clear signature of 2-nt 3′ overhangs (overhang length = 2) and perfect base-pairing (overhang length = 0), characteristic of endo-siRNAs (Rebuttal Figure. 2a). Applying the same pipeline to short-piRNAs identified in this study revealed no obvious 2-nt 3′ overhangs or perfect complementarity signature (Rebuttal Figure. 2b). Instead, these short-piRNAs exhibited canonical piRNA features, including a strong 1U and 10A bias (Supplementary Fig. 4c), a 10-nt Ping-Pong signature (Supplementary Fig. 4d).
Rebuttal Figure 2. Analysis of 3′ overhang signature for endo-siRNAs in mouse MII oocytes and short-piRNAs in human oocytes.
(a) Distribution of endo-siRNAs (20-24 nt) with varying 3’-end overhang lengths in mouse MII oocytes. Data represent pooled endo-siRNAs from 5 oocyte samples.
(b) Distribution of short-piRNAs (17-24 nt) with varying 3’-end overhang lengths in PrF, PF, GV, and MII oocytes. Data represent pooled short-piRNAs derived from 4-9 oocytes across different developmental stages. In both (a) and (b), Z-scores for overhang lengths of 0 nt (Z0) and 2 nt (Z2) are shown and calculated with overhang lengths of 1 and 3-20 nt used as background.
Together, these results demonstrate that short-piRNAs characterized in our study are bona fide PIWIL3-associated piRNAs that lack 2′-O-methylation at their 3’ ends across multiple oocyte stages.
2. Figure 1f (line 136-144): The authors show that L1PA2 has undergone a 128.90-fold downregulation while HERV-L and HERV-K have exhibited a 89.43-fold and a 29.50-fold repression, respectively. The authors should show expression levels of corresponding piRNAs (just like Figure 4e). This will help the reader understand the relationship between expression levels of piRNAs and degree of TE repression.
Response: We analyzed the relationship between TE expression changes and the corresponding levels of short- and long-piRNAs, with strand specificity, focusing on L1PA2, HERV-L, and HERV-K. Our analysis revealed that the downregulation of L1PA2 was significantly correlated with an increase in both sense and antisense short-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 9b). In contrast, L1PA2-related sense and antisense long-piRNAs decreased during human oocyte development. For HERV-L, its downregulation was accompanied by an increase in both short- and long-piRNAs, independent of strand orientation (Supplementary Fig. 9c), suggesting a coordinated role for both piRNA classes in repressing this element. For HERV-K, only sense short-piRNAs showed a marked increase from the PrF to the MII stage, and this increase was significantly correlated with reduced HERV-K transcript abundance (Supplementary Fig. 9d). In addition, we examined the expression changes of L1HS, AluYb8, and SVA_A, along with their corresponding short- and long-piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 9a, e, and f).
Collectively, these results support the conclusion that short- and long-piRNAs may play distinct, TE subfamily-specific regulatory roles during human oocyte maturation. These new analyses have been incorporated into the revised Supplementary Fig. 9 and are described in the corresponding Results section (Line 316-329) of the revised manuscript.
Supplementary Figure 9. Relationship between piRNA abundance and the extent of TE downregulation.
(a-f) Scatter plots showing the correlations between TE expression levels and the abundance of their corresponding short- and long-piRNA in developing human oocytes for L1HS (a), L1PA2 (b), HERVL (c), HERVK (d), AluYb8 (e), and SVA A (f). Pearson correlation coefficients (R) and p-values (p) are shown in each panel.
3. Figure 1f: Some group of ERVs are upregulated during oocyte development. What might distinguish this group of TEs from other TEs which are downregulated during oocyte development. Are these TEs located in piRNA clusters identified in this study?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We examined multiple characteristics of upregulated and downregulated TE subfamilies, including related short- and long-piRNA abundance, Ping-Pong Z-scores, 1U and 10A ratios, and TE transcript levels. We found that upregulated TE subfamilies displayed significantly higher transcript levels than downregulated TE subfamilies (Supplementary Fig. 10a). However, apart from this higher-level in transcript abundance, all other piRNA-related signatures were markedly lower in upregulated TE subfamilies—most notably, the abundance of corresponding antisense short- and long-piRNAs. Consistently, upregulated TE subfamilies exhibited weaker Ping-Pong signatures, reflected by reduced 10-nt overlap ratios and 1U/10A biases.
Supplementary Figure 10. Comparative characteristics of up- and down-regulated TE subfamilies.
(a) Comparison of up- and down-regulated TE subfamilies based on related piRNA abundance, Ping-Pong Z-scores, 1U and 10A ratios, and TE transcript levels.
(b) Boxplots showing the density of upregulated and downregulated TE insertions within the top 20 piRNA clusters, separated by strand orientation (Antisense vs. Sense). For both (a) and (b), statistical significance was calculated using a t-test.
We next analyzed the genomic distribution of upregulated and downregulated TE subfamilies within the top 20 piRNA clusters, which collectively generate over 90% of uniquely mapped piRNAs. Although upregulated TE subfamilies were present within these clusters, their antisense insertions were significantly less frequent than those of the downregulated TE subfamilies, consistent with their reduced antisense short- and long-piRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 10b). Notably, seven out of the eight upregulated TE subfamilies are human-specific elements. Given their relatively high transcript abundance and reduced antisense piRNA expression, we propose that these upregulated elements likely represent evolutionarily younger TE subfamilies for which the piRNA/PIWI pathway has not yet fully adapted to achieve efficient repression—potentially due to insufficient antisense insertions within highly productive piRNA clusters.
These new analyses have been incorporated into the revised Supplementary Fig. 10 and are described in the corresponding Results section (Line 333-341) of the revised manuscript, which reads as:
“Compared with TE subfamilies that were downregulated, these upregulated TE subfamilies showed higher transcript abundance but produced markedly fewer corresponding antisense and sense short- and long-piRNAs, accompanied by weaker Ping-Pong signatures and reduced 1U and 10A biases (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Genomic distribution analyses within the top 20 piRNA clusters further revealed substantially fewer antisense insertions for these upregulated TE subfamilies relative to downregulated TE subfamilies, consistent with their reduced antisense piRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 10b)”.
4. Line 166: “3’-O-methylation” should be “2’-O-methylation at the 3’ end.” The authors should describe methods used to examine the presence/absence of this modification. This reviewer cannot find methods used in Methods.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this error. It has been corrected to “2’-O-methylation at the 3’ end” in the revised manuscript.
In the original version, we did not perform oxidation treatment followed by small RNA sequencing to assess the presence or absence of 2’-O-methylation, as our previous studies had already shown that short-piRNAs in GV and MII oocytes lack this modification, whereas long-piRNAs possess it (1, 2). The initial description was therefore based on these published findings. Moreover, oocytes at the early follicular stages yield extremely limited amounts of RNA, and human oocytes are particularly precious, making oxidation-based library construction technically challenging. Nevertheless, to further strengthen the rigor of the present study, we collected oocytes at the primordial and primary follicular stages and performed oxidation sequencing. Comparison between oxidized and non-oxidized samples revealed that short-piRNAs were largely depleted upon oxidation, whereas long-piRNAs were largely retained, particularly in PF-stage oocytes (Fig. 2e). These data confirm that, in oocytes at the primordial and primary follicular stages, PIWIL3-associated short-piRNAs lack 2′-O-methylation at their 3′ ends, whereas long-piRNAs possess this modification, consistent with our previous observations in GV and MII oocytes (1, 2). The incomplete depletion of short-piRNAs is likely due to the extremely limited input RNAs (approximately 2.5 oocytes per reaction), which may reduce the efficiency of the oxidation treatment.
Figure 2. piRNAs are the predominant small non-coding RNAs during human oogenesis.
(e) Length profiles of small RNAs before and after oxidation treatment in primordial follicle oocytes. Short-piRNAs (17-24 nt) were largely depleted upon oxidation, whereas long-piRNAs (25-35 nt) were largely retained, confirming the absence of 2’-O-methylation in short-piRNAs and its presence in long-piRNAs. Approximately 2.5 oocytes were pooled per sample for each oxidation assay.
These new results have been included in the revised Figure 2e and described in the Results section (Line 173-179) in the revised manuscript. The corresponding experimental details have been provided in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 541-551).
5. Figure 4f: It is peculiar that the authors do not cite the paper of Ishino et al. (NAR 49, 2700-2720, 2021) and discuss the discrepancy between the two studies. Ishino et al. conclude that most of the piRNAs expressed in oocytes are not involved in the ping-pong cycle.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important reference. We note a key methodological difference between the two studies. Ishino et al. analyzed all piRNA sequences associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-cell embryos, and reported no appreciable A enrichment at the 10th position or 10-nt overlaps between sense and antisense piRNAs. Based on these genome-wide analyses, they concluded that PIWIL1- and PIWIL3-bound piRNAs exhibit minimal or no Ping-Pong activity. In contrast, our study specifically focused on TE-related piRNAs. Because most genomic TE copies are truncated or inactive, we mapped piRNAs to consensus TE sequences downloaded from Repbase, which represent reconstructed ancestral active elements. This approach enables a more targeted evaluation of potentially active TEs and their associated piRNA signatures, which may not be detectable when analyzing the whole piRNA population.
To directly address this discrepancy, we reanalyzed the data of Ishino et al. by using both strategies: (i) all piRNA sequences, (as in Ishino et al.), and (ii) piRNAs mapped to consensus TE sequences (as used in this study and our previous work) (1, 3, 4). Consistent with Ishino et al., the nucleotide bias analysis using all piRNA sequences showed very weak or no 10A enrichment (Rebuttal Figure 3a). In contrast, the analysis based on consensus TE sequences revealed a modest but detectable 10A bias across all examined samples (Rebuttal Figure 3b). Consistently, piRNAs mapped to the sense and antisense strands of consensus TEs exhibited an obvious 10-nt overlap, indicating the presence of a low-level Ping-Pong signature (Rebuttal Figure 3c).
Together, these results suggest that the apparent discrepancy between our findings and those of Ishino et al. primarily arises from differences in analytical strategy.
Rebuttal Figure 3. Ping-Pong signature analysis for the dataset of Ishino et al.
(a) Nucleotide enrichment analysis of all piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage.
(b) Nucleotide enrichment analysis for consensus TE-aligned piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage.
(c) Ping-Pong overlap distributions of consensus TE-aligned sense and antisense piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage. Z-scores for 10-nt overlaps (Z10) were calculated by using positions 0-9 and 11-20 as background and are shown in each panel.
6. Figure 4f: L1 subfamilies are largely divided into two subgroups in terms of the z-score of ping-pong signature (high vs low). Why? Is the low z-score due to the primary processing? Is there any peculiarity of piRNAs in this group?
Response: To investigate the differences between L1 subfamilies with high (Group A) and low (Group B) Ping-Pong signatures (Supplementary Fig. 5a), we systematically analyzed nine features for Group A and B, including related short- and long-piRNA expression levels, overall 1U and 10A ratios, Ping-Pong Z-scores of short- and long-piRNAs, and the corresponding transcript abundances. L1 subfamilies with stronger Ping-Pong signatures (Group A) exhibited consistently higher values across all examined features than those with weaker Ping-Pong signatures (Group B) Supplementary Fig. 5b). As the reviewer noted, short-piRNAs in Group A displayed more pronounced Ping-Pong signatures than those in Group B, and a similar but weaker trend was also observed for long-piRNAs. This pattern was further supported by a higher 10A ratio observed in Group A. Moreover, the transcript abundance of L1 subfamilies in Group A, as well as the expression levels of their corresponding sense and antisense piRNAs, was significantly higher than in Group B.
All these observations suggest that the elevated levels of both antisense and sense piRNAs, together with the greater availability of TE transcripts as Ping-Pong substrates in Group A, promote more efficient Ping-Pong amplification.
Supplementary Figure 5. Comparative features of L1 subgroups with high and low Ping-Pong signatures
(a) Classification of L1 subfamilies into Group A (high Ping-Pong Z-scores) and Group B (low Ping-Pong Z-scores).
(b) Comparison of nine features between Group A and Group B L1 subfamilies, including related short- and long-piRNA expression levels, overall 1U and 10A ratios, Ping-Pong Z-scores of short and long-piRNAs, and the corresponding transcript abundances.
(c) Distribution of sense and antisense insertions of L1 subfamilies from Group A and B within the top 20 piRNA clusters. For both (b) and (c), statistical significance was calculated using a t-test.
Finally, we examined the genomic distribution of L1 subfamilies from Group A and B within the top 20 piRNA clusters. Interestingly, Group B showed a higher proportion of antisense insertions compared to Group A, while sense insertions displayed no significant difference (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Given the lower levels of both antisense and sense piRNA in Group B, these results suggest that primary processing and subsequent PIWI loading may preferentially promote corresponding piRNA generation in Group A. However, we cannot exclude the possibility that a fraction of antisense and sense piRNAs in Group A also arises from Ping-Pong amplification.
Collectively, these analyses indicate that the reduced Ping-Pong signature observed in certain L1 subfamilies is likely due to their lower transcript abundance and limited antisense and sense piRNA generation through primary processing.
These new analyses have been incorporated into the revised Supplementary Fig. 5 and are described in the corresponding Results section (Line 270-280) of the revised manuscript, which reads as:
“Notably, approximately two-thirds of L1 subfamilies exhibited strong Ping-Pong activity (Group A) and consistently showed higher 1U and 10A proportions, greater antisense and sense piRNA abundance, and elevated transcript levels compared with those with low signals (Group B) (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Interestingly, genomic analysis of the top 20 piRNA clusters revealed that Group B L1 subfamilies carried more antisense insertions than Group A, while sense insertions were comparable (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Given the lower abundance of both antisense and sense piRNAs for Group B, these results suggest that primary processing and PIWI loading preferentially enhance piRNA biogenesis from Group A L1 subfamilies. These findings indicate that weak Ping-Pong activity in certain L1 subfamilies likely reflects their lower transcript abundance and inefficient primary piRNA processing.”
7. Figure 6a-d (line 311-313): The authors claim a strong bias toward L1 and ERV fragments within the top 20 clusters. However, 11 out of the top 20 clusters show L1 antisense bias, which does not seem statistically strong. Could these data imply that piRNA clusters are differentially expressed at each stage of oocyte development? Do piRNA cluster share common promoters/transcription factor binding sites in a stage-specific manner, for example?
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. As the reviewer noted, although L1 showed higher antisense piRNA production than sense piRNA production in the top 20 piRNA clusters, particularly within the top 10 clusters, they do not display a clear antisense insertion bias when directly compared with their sense insertions. We have therefore revised the description to more accurately reflect this point, as now stated:
“Interestingly, although L1 elements did not show a pronounced difference in antisense versus sense insertion frequencies, the top 10 piRNA clusters still produced markedly more antisense than sense piRNAs (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Fig. 12a). This suggests selective primary processing, in which L1 antisense piRNAs may be preferentially generated or more efficiently loaded onto PIWI proteins.” (Lines 376–381).
As the reviewer noted, piRNA clusters are indeed differentially expressed during oocyte development, and their contributions to the TE-related piRNA population vary by stage. For example, the cluster chr4:78106722–78396420|+ contributed the second-largest number of L1-related antisense short-piRNAs at the PrF/PF stages but became the predominant source at the GV/MII stages. Similarly, the cluster chr12:114437233–114625671|− ranked second for ERV-related antisense short-piRNA production at the PrF stage but became the leading contributor after the PF stage. These examples have been added to the revised manuscript to further support our conclusion that piRNA clusters are differentially expressed and dynamically regulated across oocyte developmental stages, as now stated:
“These clusters displayed dynamic expression patterns during oocyte development, with their contributions to TE-related piRNA population varying by stage (Fig. 6a, b, and Supplementary Data 9). For example, the cluster chr4:78106722–78396420|+ ranked second for L1 antisense short-piRNA generation at the PrF and PF stages, but became the predominant source at the GV/MII stages. Similarly, the cluster chr12:114437233–114625671|− produced the second-largest number of ERV antisense short piRNAs at the PrF stage and emerged as the primary contributor after the PF stage.” (Lines 356-363).
piRNA clusters are generally defined as genomic regions enriched for piRNAs, although their primary transcripts are often difficult to delineate due to extensive precursor processing. Previous work (5) demonstrated that bidirectional piRNA clusters are particularly informative for identifying promoters and associated transcription factors. That study further showed that A-MYB acts as a key transcriptional regulator of pachytene piRNA biogenesis and PIWIL1 expression during mouse spermatogenesis, with a conserved role in other species.
In our analysis of the top 20 piRNA clusters, we identified 2 pairs of bidirectional clusters (chr5:73361914–73441831|– vs chr5:73438508–73512499|+, and chr6:39934078–40135208|– vs chr6:40129348–40169244|+) (Supplementary Fig. 11). Notably, one of these four loci (chr6:40129348–40169244|+) was ranked outside the top 20 based on relatively lower unique piRNA generation. Expanding the analysis to the top 100 piRNA clusters revealed two additional pairs of bidirectional clusters. These findings suggest that, unlike pachytene piRNAs in mouse testis, only a small subset of human oocyte piRNA clusters originates from bidirectionally transcribed loci, consistent with previous observations in golden hamster oocytes (6). Among the four bidirectional pairs identified within the top 100 piRNA clusters, two appear to arise from back-to-back transcribed primary transcripts (chr5:73361914–73441831|– vs chr5:73438508–73512499|+; chr6:39934078–40135208|– vs chr6:40129348–40169244|+), which may share common promoter or transcription factor binding regions. We analyzed these shared regions to predict potential motifs or regulatory factors; however, no significantly enriched motifs were detected, likely due to the limited sequence regions available for analysis.
We have added the genome browser views for these two back-to-back transcribed piRNA clusters in revised Supplementary Fig. 11, and a description of this observation into the revised manuscript:
“Notably, only two pairs of bidirectionally transcribed clusters were identified among the top 20 piRNA clusters (Supplementary Fig. 11), and expanding the analysis to the top 100 clusters revealed two additional pairs. This indicates that, in contrast to pachytene piRNAs in mouse testis (5), only a small fraction of human oocyte piRNA clusters arises from bidirectionally transcribed loci, consistent with observations in golden hamster oocytes (6).” (Lines 363–369).
