Approximately 2.5 oocytes were pooled per sample for each oxidation assay.
These new results have been included in the revised Figure 2e and described in the Results section (Line 173-179) in the revised manuscript. The corresponding experimental details have been provided in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 541-551).
5. Figure 4f: It is peculiar that the authors do not cite the paper of Ishino et al. (NAR 49, 2700-2720, 2021) and discuss the discrepancy between the two studies. Ishino et al. conclude that most of the piRNAs expressed in oocytes are not involved in the ping-pong cycle.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this important reference. We note a key methodological difference between the two studies. Ishino et al. analyzed all piRNA sequences associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-cell embryos, and reported no appreciable A enrichment at the 10th position or 10-nt overlaps between sense and antisense piRNAs. Based on these genome-wide analyses, they concluded that PIWIL1- and PIWIL3-bound piRNAs exhibit minimal or no Ping-Pong activity. In contrast, our study specifically focused on TE-related piRNAs. Because most genomic TE copies are truncated or inactive, we mapped piRNAs to consensus TE sequences downloaded from Repbase, which represent reconstructed ancestral active elements. This approach enables a more targeted evaluation of potentially active TEs and their associated piRNA signatures, which may not be detectable when analyzing the whole piRNA population.
To directly address this discrepancy, we reanalyzed the data of Ishino et al. by using both strategies: (i) all piRNA sequences, (as in Ishino et al.), and (ii) piRNAs mapped to consensus TE sequences (as used in this study and our previous work) (1, 3, 4). Consistent with Ishino et al., the nucleotide bias analysis using all piRNA sequences showed very weak or no 10A enrichment (Rebuttal Figure 3a). In contrast, the analysis based on consensus TE sequences revealed a modest but detectable 10A bias across all examined samples (Rebuttal Figure 3b). Consistently, piRNAs mapped to the sense and antisense strands of consensus TEs exhibited an obvious 10-nt overlap, indicating the presence of a low-level Ping-Pong signature (Rebuttal Figure 3c).
Together, these results suggest that the apparent discrepancy between our findings and those of Ishino et al. primarily arises from differences in analytical strategy.
Rebuttal Figure 3. Ping-Pong signature analysis for the dataset of Ishino et al.
(a) Nucleotide enrichment analysis of all piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage.
(b) Nucleotide enrichment analysis for consensus TE-aligned piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage.
(c) Ping-Pong overlap distributions of consensus TE-aligned sense and antisense piRNAs associated with PIWIL1 and PIWIL3 in hamster testis, ovary, MII oocytes, and 2-Cell embryonic stage. Z-scores for 10-nt overlaps (Z10) were calculated by using positions 0-9 and 11-20 as background and are shown in each panel.
6. Figure 4f: L1 subfamilies are largely divided into two subgroups in terms of the z-score of ping-pong signature (high vs low). Why? Is the low z-score due to the primary processing? Is there any peculiarity of piRNAs in this group?
Response: To investigate the differences between L1 subfamilies with high (Group A) and low (Group B) Ping-Pong signatures (Supplementary Fig. 5a), we systematically analyzed nine features for Group A and B, including related short- and long-piRNA expression levels, overall 1U and 10A ratios, Ping-Pong Z-scores of short- and long-piRNAs, and the corresponding transcript abundances. L1 subfamilies with stronger Ping-Pong signatures (Group A) exhibited consistently higher values across all examined features than those with weaker Ping-Pong signatures (Group B) Supplementary Fig. 5b). As the reviewer noted, short-piRNAs in Group A displayed more pronounced Ping-Pong signatures than those in Group B, and a similar but weaker trend was also observed for long-piRNAs. This pattern was further supported by a higher 10A ratio observed in Group A. Moreover, the transcript abundance of L1 subfamilies in Group A, as well as the expression levels of their corresponding sense and antisense piRNAs, was significantly higher than in Group B.
All these observations suggest that the elevated levels of both antisense and sense piRNAs, together with the greater availability of TE transcripts as Ping-Pong substrates in Group A, promote more efficient Ping-Pong amplification.
Supplementary Figure 5. Comparative features of L1 subgroups with high and low Ping-Pong signatures
(a) Classification of L1 subfamilies into Group A (high Ping-Pong Z-scores) and Group B (low Ping-Pong Z-scores).
(b) Comparison of nine features between Group A and Group B L1 subfamilies, including related short- and long-piRNA expression levels, overall 1U and 10A ratios, Ping-Pong Z-scores of short and long-piRNAs, and the corresponding transcript abundances.
(c) Distribution of sense and antisense insertions of L1 subfamilies from Group A and B within the top 20 piRNA clusters. For both (b) and (c), statistical significance was calculated using a t-test.
Finally, we examined the genomic distribution of L1 subfamilies from Group A and B within the top 20 piRNA clusters. Interestingly, Group B showed a higher proportion of antisense insertions compared to Group A, while sense insertions displayed no significant difference (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Given the lower levels of both antisense and sense piRNA in Group B, these results suggest that primary processing and subsequent PIWI loading may preferentially promote corresponding piRNA generation in Group A. However, we cannot exclude the possibility that a fraction of antisense and sense piRNAs in Group A also arises from Ping-Pong amplification.
Collectively, these analyses indicate that the reduced Ping-Pong signature observed in certain L1 subfamilies is likely due to their lower transcript abundance and limited antisense and sense piRNA generation through primary processing.
These new analyses have been incorporated into the revised Supplementary Fig. 5 and are described in the corresponding Results section (Line 270-280) of the revised manuscript, which reads as:
“Notably, approximately two-thirds of L1 subfamilies exhibited strong Ping-Pong activity (Group A) and consistently showed higher 1U and 10A proportions, greater antisense and sense piRNA abundance, and elevated transcript levels compared with those with low signals (Group B) (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Interestingly, genomic analysis of the top 20 piRNA clusters revealed that Group B L1 subfamilies carried more antisense insertions than Group A, while sense insertions were comparable (Supplementary Fig. 5c). Given the lower abundance of both antisense and sense piRNAs for Group B, these results suggest that primary processing and PIWI loading preferentially enhance piRNA biogenesis from Group A L1 subfamilies. These findings indicate that weak Ping-Pong activity in certain L1 subfamilies likely reflects their lower transcript abundance and inefficient primary piRNA processing.”
7. Figure 6a-d (line 311-313): The authors claim a strong bias toward L1 and ERV fragments within the top 20 clusters. However, 11 out of the top 20 clusters show L1 antisense bias, which does not seem statistically strong. Could these data imply that piRNA clusters are differentially expressed at each stage of oocyte development? Do piRNA cluster share common promoters/transcription factor binding sites in a stage-specific manner, for example?
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. As the reviewer noted, although L1 showed higher antisense piRNA production than sense piRNA production in the top 20 piRNA clusters, particularly within the top 10 clusters, they do not display a clear antisense insertion bias when directly compared with their sense insertions. We have therefore revised the description to more accurately reflect this point, as now stated:
“Interestingly, although L1 elements did not show a pronounced difference in antisense versus sense insertion frequencies, the top 10 piRNA clusters still produced markedly more antisense than sense piRNAs (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Fig. 12a). This suggests selective primary processing, in which L1 antisense piRNAs may be preferentially generated or more efficiently loaded onto PIWI proteins.” (Lines 376–381).
As the reviewer noted, piRNA clusters are indeed differentially expressed during oocyte development, and their contributions to the TE-related piRNA population vary by stage. For example, the cluster chr4:78106722–78396420|+ contributed the second-largest number of L1-related antisense short-piRNAs at the PrF/PF stages but became the predominant source at the GV/MII stages. Similarly, the cluster chr12:114437233–114625671|− ranked second for ERV-related antisense short-piRNA production at the PrF stage but became the leading contributor after the PF stage. These examples have been added to the revised manuscript to further support our conclusion that piRNA clusters are differentially expressed and dynamically regulated across oocyte developmental stages, as now stated:
“These clusters displayed dynamic expression patterns during oocyte development, with their contributions to TE-related piRNA population varying by stage (Fig. 6a, b, and Supplementary Data 9). For example, the cluster chr4:78106722–78396420|+ ranked second for L1 antisense short-piRNA generation at the PrF and PF stages, but became the predominant source at the GV/MII stages. Similarly, the cluster chr12:114437233–114625671|− produced the second-largest number of ERV antisense short piRNAs at the PrF stage and emerged as the primary contributor after the PF stage.” (Lines 356-363).
piRNA clusters are generally defined as genomic regions enriched for piRNAs, although their primary transcripts are often difficult to delineate due to extensive precursor processing. Previous work (5) demonstrated that bidirectional piRNA clusters are particularly informative for identifying promoters and associated transcription factors. That study further showed that A-MYB acts as a key transcriptional regulator of pachytene piRNA biogenesis and PIWIL1 expression during mouse spermatogenesis, with a conserved role in other species.
In our analysis of the top 20 piRNA clusters, we identified 2 pairs of bidirectional clusters (chr5:73361914–73441831|– vs chr5:73438508–73512499|+, and chr6:39934078–40135208|– vs chr6:40129348–40169244|+) (Supplementary Fig. 11). Notably, one of these four loci (chr6:40129348–40169244|+) was ranked outside the top 20 based on relatively lower unique piRNA generation. Expanding the analysis to the top 100 piRNA clusters revealed two additional pairs of bidirectional clusters. These findings suggest that, unlike pachytene piRNAs in mouse testis, only a small subset of human oocyte piRNA clusters originates from bidirectionally transcribed loci, consistent with previous observations in golden hamster oocytes (6). Among the four bidirectional pairs identified within the top 100 piRNA clusters, two appear to arise from back-to-back transcribed primary transcripts (chr5:73361914–73441831|– vs chr5:73438508–73512499|+; chr6:39934078–40135208|– vs chr6:40129348–40169244|+), which may share common promoter or transcription factor binding regions. We analyzed these shared regions to predict potential motifs or regulatory factors; however, no significantly enriched motifs were detected, likely due to the limited sequence regions available for analysis.
We have added the genome browser views for these two back-to-back transcribed piRNA clusters in revised Supplementary Fig. 11, and a description of this observation into the revised manuscript:
“Notably, only two pairs of bidirectionally transcribed clusters were identified among the top 20 piRNA clusters (Supplementary Fig. 11), and expanding the analysis to the top 100 clusters revealed two additional pairs. This indicates that, in contrast to pachytene piRNAs in mouse testis (5), only a small fraction of human oocyte piRNA clusters arises from bidirectionally transcribed loci, consistent with observations in golden hamster oocytes (6).” (Lines 363–369).
Supplementary Figure 11. UCSC genome browser views of two back-to-back transcribed piRNA clusters
(a) Genome browser view of back-to-back transcribed piRNA cluster pair (chr5:73361914 - 73441831|– vs chr5:73438508 - 73512499|+), showing the surrounding gene annotations, density of TE superfamily insertions, long RNA-seq signal, and expression levels of uniquely and total mapped short- and long-piRNAs.
(b) Genome browser view of back-to-back transcribed piRNA cluster pair (chr6:39934078–40135208|– vs chr6:40129348–40169244|+), showing the surrounding gene annotations, density of TE superfamily insertions, long RNA-seq signal, and expression levels of uniquely and total mapped short- and long-piRNAs.
Strand-specific piRNA read coverage on opposing strands reveals convergent transcription and reciprocal processing, characteristic of bidirectional piRNA cluster organization. Long RNA-seq signal is strand-unspecific.
8. Figure 6e: How do the authors know that the piRNA cluster is unidirectionally transcribed? Are short-piRNAs produced by the ping-pong cycle derived from unidirectionally transcribed cluster transcripts?
Response: In the current version of the manuscript, we did not specifically discuss the transcriptional orientation of piRNA clusters following their identification. Our identification strategy was based on detecting regions enriched for piRNAs mapped to the same strand, and regions containing more than five unique piRNAs were defined as piRNA clusters.
As described in our response to Question 7, we identified 3 bidirectional piRNA clusters among the top 20 clusters, with the remaining 17 classified as unidirectional. We next examined the origin of short-piRNAs involved in the Ping-Pong amplification cycle relative to bidirectional and unidirectional cluster types. Our analysis showed that over 75% of TE-related short-piRNAs exhibiting a characteristic 10-nt overlap were derived from unidirectional clusters, whereas fewer than 25% originated from the bidirectional clusters (Rebuttal Figure. 4a). A similar distribution was observed for long-piRNAs, indicating that both short- and long-piRNAs with Ping-Pong signatures are predominantly generated from unidirectional clusters (Rebuttal Figure. 4b). It is important to note that many piRNAs with 10-nt overlaps are multi-mapped; therefore, all mapped piRNAs were included in this analysis, which means may lead to partial overlap between piRNAs assigned to unidirectional versus bidirectional clusters.
Rebuttal Figure 4. Proportion of TE-related short- (a) and long-piRNAs (b) with 10-nt overlap signatures derived from the top 20 unidirectional and bidirectional piRNA clusters. All piRNAs (uniquely and multiply mapped) were included in the analysis.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Integrated small and long RNA sequencing in single oocytes reveals piRNA-mediated transposon repression during human oogenesis
The manuscript describes the expression, by nucleotide sequencing, of small non coding RNAs, mRNAs and transposon elements in human oocytes of 4 different developmental stages: primordial follicle, primary follicle, germinal vesicle and metaphase II. It is concluded that short piwi interacting RNAs (piRNAs) act as primary suppressors of transposon activity, while long piRNAS coordinate silencing of specific ERV transposons.
In general, the manuscript provides a nice descriptive dataset of expressed piRNA and transposon sequences at different stage of human oocytes. In that respect it is of value to the scientific community.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript. We are encouraged that the reviewer considers our dataset valuable to the scientific community and appreciates the comprehensive characterization of piRNAs and transposon dynamics across human oocyte development. We also thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and suggestions regarding additional analyses and clarifications that could enhance the biological significance of our study. We have carefully revised the manuscript in response to these points. Below, we provide a point-by-point response, highlighting the changes made to the text, figures, and supplementary materials where appropriate.
Functional data that demonstrate the activity of certain piRNAs, or how possible transposon activity would affect the quality of the oocyte or a possible developing embryo are lacking however. This limits the conclusions that can be drawn from the data, and as such it is merely a descriptive manuscript. There may be correlation, but there is no demonstration of a causation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the important distinction between correlation and causation, and for pointing out the limitations arising from the absence of direct functional perturbation experiments. We agree that functional assays would provide definitive evidence for the mechanistic roles of short- and long-piRNAs in transposon regulation. However, such experiments remain technically and ethically challenging in human oocytes. Given these constraints, our study aims to establish a foundational, high-resolution atlas of piRNA populations and TE expression, and to propose a potential regulatory model supported by multiple, independent lines of correlative evidence. We have now revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge this limitation and to emphasize the need for further functional, clinical, or genetic studies to further elucidate the consequences of PIWI/piRNA pathway activity on TE regulation, as stated:
“Second, definitive functional validation will be required to establish the causal roles of piRNAs in human oocyte development. However, such experiments remain largely infeasible due to the extremely limited availability of human oocytes and strict ethical constraints. Even so, evidence from model organisms shows that disruption of piRNA biogenesis leads to defective oocyte development and early embryonic arrest (7-11), underscoring the central importance of this pathway. Future clinical and genetic studies will therefore be critical to elucidate the functional consequences of PIWI/piRNA dysfunction in human reproductive biology.” (Lines 475–482).
Major comments.
The analysis of piRNA, PIWI protein genes and transposon expression of human oocytes at different developmental stages is solid, well described and well presented in clear figures. The sequencing, though solid and extensive, is not novel. Similar data have been published previously eg PMID: 34340992; PMID: 33622565; PMID: 25818294; PMID: 31358756.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the positive comments on our data analysis and for noting that previous studies have profiled small RNAs during human oogenesis and early embryonic development. However, we believe that our study provides at least two important advances beyond these earlier efforts.
1. Integrated profiling of small and long RNAs simultaneously at the single-oocyte level. Our dataset simultaneously profiles both small and long RNAs from the same individual human oocytes, allowing integrated analyses of small regulatory RNAs, including piRNAs and miRNAs, together with long transcripts, such as protein-coding mRNAs and transposable element transcripts. This approach enables a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the relationships between small RNAs and their targets at single-oocyte resolution.
2. Comprehensive developmental coverage, particularly follicular stages. Our dataset encompasses four key stages of human oogenesis—primordial follicle, primary follicle, germinal vesicle, and metaphase II—providing a broader temporal view of both small and long RNA dynamics. As the reviewer may note, small RNA datasets for human oocytes at the follicular stages have been largely unavailable. Characterizing small RNAs during these early developmental stages is crucial for understanding transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation underlying follicle activation and growth, offering valuable insights into follicle recruitment and the restoration of oocyte competence. The lack of such datasets likely reflects the extreme scarcity of early-stage human oocytes and the low abundance of small RNAs at these stages, which require highly sensitive library construction methods. To overcome these challenges, in this study, we optimized our small RNA library construction protocol to make it suitable for early-stage human oocytes.
Together, these features make our dataset a unique and valuable resource for studying human oogenesis, providing integrated, stage-resolved, single-oocyte–level insights into small RNA functions and their potential regulatory roles in gene expression and transposable element control. We have revised the Discussion section to emphasize the novelty and uniqueness of our dataset, highlighting its advantage compared with previously published human oocyte datasets. The added text now reads:
“Unlike previous studies that examined only small RNAs during human oogenesis and early embryonic development (2, 12, 13), our approach integrates matched small- and long-RNA sequencing from the same individual oocytes, including the previously underrepresented PrF and PF stages. This design provides a unified view of RNA regulation—from small RNA biogenesis and TE transcripts or mRNA expression dynamics—providing unprecedented resolution for investigating stage-specific small RNA-mediated regulatory processes in human oocytes.” (Line 420-426).
Functional data are lacking in the manuscript. In that sense it is descriptive, and conclusions drawn are rather speculative. Different interpretations of the data are possible, and how presence of absence of piRNAs would affect the quality and functionality of oocytes remains unknown.
Response: We agree that direct functional validation would provide the strongest evidence for the role of piRNAs in human oogenesis. However, such experiments are currently infeasible due to the extremely limited availability of human oocytes, particularly those with piRNA deficiency. Notably, studies in the model organisms have provided compelling evidence that disruption of the piRNA pathway leads to abnormal oocyte development and early embryonic arrest. We and two other groups independently established golden hamsters as a mammalian model for piRNA-related research and demonstrated that oocytes lacking piRNAs fail to support embryogenesis (4, 8, 14). Specifically, disruption of PIWIL1-associated long-piRNAs resulted in developmental arrest at the 2-cell stage, whereas loss of PIWIL3-associated short-piRNAs caused partial arrest between the 2- and 8-cell stages. More recently, a study from Dr. Haifan Lin’s group, using rabbits as an animal model, showed that depletion of PIWIL3-associated short-piRNAs leads to complete infertility, accompanied by severe defects in both oocyte maturation and early embryonic development (11). Together, these findings support a conserved and essential role for piRNAs in mammalian oogenesis and embryogenesis.
Although direct functional evidence in human oocytes remains unavailable, these results from model organisms strongly suggest that piRNAs play a crucial role in maintaining oocyte quality and developmental competence. We have revised the Discussion section to acknowledge this limitation and clarify that our study provides correlative rather than functional evidence for the role of piRNAs in human oogenesis. The revised text reads:
“Second, definitive functional validation will be required to establish the causal roles of piRNAs in human oocyte development. However, such experiments remain largely infeasible due to the extremely limited availability of human oocytes and strict ethical constraints. Even so, evidence from model organisms shows that disruption of piRNA biogenesis leads to defective oocyte development and early embryonic arrest (7-11), underscoring the central importance of this pathway. Future clinical and genetic studies will therefore be critical to elucidate the functional consequences of PIWI/piRNA dysfunction in human reproductive biology.” (Lines 475–482).
Although in the introduction it is mentioned that in mice oocytes transposon activity is thought to be regulated via miRNAs and a specific Dicer isoform, crucial information here that the mouse genome does not harbour Piwil3 should be mentioned.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have revised the Introduction section to explicitly note that the mouse genome lacks the Piwil3 gene. The revised text now reads:
“Interestingly, the Piwil3 gene is absent from the mouse genome and mouse oocytes primarily express endo-siRNAs rather than piRNAs” (lines 83-85)
In the results section it is stated that 30 oocytes were collected. The value of this number is limited, as only 23 oocytes were used. The numbers is Fig1A ae misleading: PrF n=7: only 5 were used, PF n=12: only 9 were used, MII n=7: only 5 were used.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. In total, 30 oocytes were collected and sequenced, including 7 primordial follicle (PrF), 12 primary follicle (PF), 4 germinal vesicle (GV), and 7 metaphase II (MII) stage oocytes. However, simultaneous profiling of small and long RNAs from the same single oocyte remains technically challenging, and not all paired libraries passed our quality control (QC) criteria. To ensure high-quality data for downstream analysis, we applied stringent QC filters to both the small RNA and long RNA datasets.
For small RNA libraries, we excluded samples with (i) a useful read rate below 60% after 3′ adaptor trimming and short-read removal, (ii) a mapped read rate below 40%, and (iii) rRNA/tRNA-derived reads exceeding 30%. For long RNA libraries, we excluded samples with (i) a mapped read rate below 80%, (ii) mitochondrial-derived reads exceeding 10%, or (iii) rRNA-derived reads exceeding 10%. After applying these QC criteria, 23 oocytes passed QC for both RNA types and were retained for downstream analyses. We have added these QC details to the revised manuscript to clarify why 23 oocytes remained, as stated:
“To ensure high data quality for downstream analysis, we applied stringent quality-control criteria to both the small RNA and long RNA datasets. For small RNA data, we removed samples with a useful read rate below 60% after 3’ adaptor trimming and short-read filtering, a mapped read rate below 40%, or rRNA/tRNA-derived reads exceeding 30%. For long RNA data, we excluded samples with a mapped read rate below 80%, mitochondrial-derived reads exceeding 10%, or rRNA-derived reads exceeding 10%.” (Lines 108-113).
Although the total number of oocytes is limited, we incorporated statistical testing across all relevant analyses following the reviewer’s suggestion. Nearly all results supporting our main conclusions reached statistical significance, indicating that the number of oocytes analyzed is sufficient to ensure the robustness of our key findings. To avoid further misunderstanding, we have updated Fig. 1a and added the number of oocytes used for library construction as well as those retained after quality filtering in the figure legend.
Figure 1. Global downregulation of TEs occurs after the primary follicle stages during human oocyte development and maturation
(a) Schematic of the experimental strategy for simultaneous profiling of small and long RNA transcriptomes from single human oocytes at four developmental stages: primordial follicle (PrF), primary follicle (PF), germinal vesicle (GV), and metaphase II (MII). A total of 7 (Prf), 12 (PF), 4 (GV), and 7 (MII) oocytes were collected at each respective stage, of which 5 (Prf), 9 (PF), 4 (GV), and 5 (MII) were retained after quality filtering.
It is not clear whether the somatic cells surrounding the oocytes (granulosa and cumulus) were removed. For the GV and MII oocytes it is evident that these were removed but for the oocytes from primordial follicles this is less clear. How certain are the authors that all somatic cells were indeed removed? Indeed, in figure 1a, the oocytes are presented with somatic cells present.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. All oocytes used for sequencing were thoroughly denuded of surrounding somatic cells, regardless of their developmental stage. We acknowledge that the previous description in the Methods section may have inadvertently suggested that this procedure was applied only to GV and MII oocytes. To avoid potential misunderstanding, we have now revised the text to explicitly state that the same denudation procedure was used for all follicular stages:
“For all oocytes at all developmental stages, surrounding granulosa and cumulus cells were removed via incubation with 1 mg/mL hyaluronidase.” (Line 504-505).
In addition, Fig. 1a has been updated to clearly indicate that granulosa and cumulus cells were removed from all oocytes prior to sequencing.
To further confirm the absence of somatic cell contamination, we now provide two lines of evidence:
1. Morphological validation: We provided representative bright-field images of oocytes before and after removal of surrounding somatic cells (Rebuttal Figure 5).
Rebuttal Figure 5. Morphology of human oocytes before and after somatic cell removal.
Representative bright-field images of human oocytes before (left), during (middle), and after (right) removal of granulosa and cumulus cells. These images demonstrate the clean isolation of denuded oocytes used for downstream small RNA and long RNA sequencing. In the middle panel, black arrows indicate removed somatic cells, and white arrows indicate the denuded oocytes. Scale bars, 50 μm.
2. Molecular validation: We additionally performed small RNA sequencing on (i) cumulus cell (CC) samples, and (ii) GV-stage oocytes surrounded by cumulus cells (GV+CC samples), which were obtained by gently needle flushing to remove most, but not all cumulus cells to avoid oocyte damage. We firstly compared the miRNA profiles between denuded GV oocytes and CC samples and identified both GV oocyte-specific and CC-specific expressed miRNAs (Rebuttal Figure. 6a). GV oocyte-specific expressed miRNAs such as miR-372, miR-516a-5p, and miR-5683 were detected in both denuded GV oocytes and GV+CC samples but absent in CC-only samples (Rebuttal Figure. 6b). Conversely, cumulus cell-specific miRNAs (miR-144-3p, miR-379-5p and miR-382-5p) were detected in CC-only and GV+CC samples but not in denuded GV oocytes and were also absent across all other oocyte stages analyzed in this study (Rebuttal Figure. 6b).
Together, these results confirm that somatic cell contamination in the oocytes used for sequencing was minimal.

(a) Differential expressed analysis for miRNAs between cumulus cells (CC) and denuded GV stage oocytes.
(b) Expression levels of cumulus cell–specific miRNAs (miR-144-3p, miR-379-5p, and miR-382-5p) in CC samples, GV oocytes surrounded by cumulus cells (GV+CC), denuded GV oocytes, and other stage oocytes (PrF, PF, and MII).
(c) Expression levels of oocyte-enriched miRNAs (miR-372, miR-516a-5p, miR-5683) across CC samples, GV+CC samples, denuded GV oocytes, and oocytes at other developmental stages (PrF, PF, and MII). Significance was calculated by t-test and is shown in each panel.
Fig 1c, and 2d, the colored areas are a bit misleading, just the colored dots would be more informative and realistic.
Response: We have updated all PCA plots in Fig. 1b-c, Fig. 2b, Fig. 2f, Fig. 4a, and Fig. 5a by removing the colored background areas while retaining the elliptical outlines to improve visual clarity and facilitate interpretation. The ellipses were generated using the stat_ellipse function in the ggplot2 R package, which provides a statistically robust representation of data dispersion.
Rebuttal Figure 7. Updated PCA plots in Fig. 1b-c, Fig. 2b, Fig. 2f, Fig. 4a and Fig. 5a
Ellipses were generated using the stat_ellipse function in the ggplot2 R package, which provides a statistically supported visualization of group dispersion.
In the different violin plots such as Fig 1g, 2c, 2e, 4b, 4d,5f, 5g indications of which data sets differ statistically from others is essential.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Statistical details have been incorporated for all relevant figure panels.
The use of the word ‘repression’ is suggestive, or misleading, as it indicates and active mechanism. For instance in line 150 where it is stated that Alu and SVA elements underwent repression with fold changes of 4.71 and 5.36. What is the indication that these elements were repressed, rather than having reduced expression? From these data there is no indication of repression. Similar for ‘robust silencing’ in line 149. There are no experimental data indicating that the expression is actively silenced, instead of expression simply being at a lower level.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree that the terms “repression” and “robust silencing” may not be fully supported by our current assays. Accordingly, we have replaced them with “reduced expression” or “downregulation,” which more accurately describe the observed decreases in TE expression levels without implying direct transcriptional or post-transcriptional silencing. We have carefully reviewed and revised the manuscript to ensure the consistent use of accurate and neutral terminology.
The manuscript is concentrated on indicating that piRNAs are important for reducing transposon activity. At the same time, expression of miRNAs, even at low levels, is suggested to ‘ contribute to oocyte development’ line 188. Although it is understandable that piRNAs are linked with suppression of TE activity, the data presented in this manuscript do not exclude that piRNA, similar to miRNAs, have another role besides repression of TE activity that is beneficial for acquiring oocyte developmental competence.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that, although TE silencing remains the best-characterized function of the piRNA pathway, growing evidence suggests that piRNAs and PIWI proteins also participate in gene regulation (15-18). In our analysis, we found that approximately 35-45% of piRNAs originate from repetitive elements, whereas ~5–10% map to annotated coding or exonic non-TE regions (Supplementary Fig. 4b). Notably, these region-aligned piRNAs lacked the characteristic 10A bias, suggesting potential roles in gene regulation through Ping-Pong–independent mechanisms (Supplementary Fig. 4c).
In the revised manuscript, we have now highlighted the presence and characteristics of these gene-derived piRNAs in the Result section, as stated:
“Although the majority of piRNAs mapped to various TE families, a notable minority (5-10%) originated from coding or other exonic non-TE genomic regions (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c). Unlike TE-related piRNAs, these piRNAs lacked the characteristic 10A bias (Supplementary Fig. 4c), suggesting they may participate in gene regulation through Ping-Pong–independent mechanisms.” (Line 283-287).
We also expanded the Discussion to address the potential regulatory roles pf these gene-aligned piRNAs during oocyte maturation and early embryogenesis, which now reads:
“This study has two important limitations. First, although TE silencing is the well-established function of the piRNA pathway (19), growing evidence indicates that piRNAs and PIWI proteins also participate in broader gene regulatory processes (15-18). Here, we did not assess whether piRNAs engage in additional regulatory mechanisms that may influence oocyte competence. Nevertheless, the single-oocyte co-sequencing dataset generated in this study provides a valuable foundation for uncovering potential noncanonical piRNA-mediated regulatory mechanisms during human oogenesis.” (Line 468-474).
On the same note, expression of several TE increase during oocyte development (line 148; fig 1f). What is the proposed function of this increased expression. Could it be important for acquisition of developmental competence?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question. To address it, we performed a comparative analysis of upregulated and downregulated TE subfamilies, examining the expression levels of sense and antisense piRNAs, the strength of Ping-Pong signatures for both short- and long-piRNAs, overall 1U/10A ratios, and TE transcript levels (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Upregulated TE subfamilies displayed significantly higher transcript levels than downregulated TE subfamilies. However, apart from their elevated transcript abundance, all other piRNA-related features were markedly lower in upregulated TEs—most notably, the abundance of corresponding antisense short- and long-piRNAs. Consistently, these up-regulated TE subfamilies exhibited weaker Ping-Pong signatures, reflected by reduced 10-nt overlap ratios and diminished 1U/10A biases.

(b) Boxplots showing the density of upregulated and downregulated TE insertions within the top 20 piRNA clusters, separated by strand orientation (Antisense vs. Sense). For both (a) and (b), statistical significance was calculated using a t-test.
We next analyzed the genomic distribution of upregulated and downregulated TE subfamilies within the top 20 piRNA clusters, which collectively generate over 90% of uniquely mapped piRNAs. Although upregulated TEs were present within these clusters, their antisense insertions were significantly less frequent than those of the downregulated TE subfamilies, consistent with their reduced antisense short- and long-piRNA expression levels (Supplementary Fig. 10b).
Notably, seven out of the eight upregulated TE subfamilies are human-specific elements. Given their relatively high transcript abundance and reduced antisense piRNA expression, we propose that these upregulated elements likely represent evolutionarily younger TE subfamilies for which the piRNA/PIWI pathway has not yet fully adapted to achieve efficient repression—potentially due to insufficient antisense insertions within highly productive piRNA clusters.
Nevertheless, we cannot exclude the possibility that increased expression of these TE subfamilies may contribute functionally to oocyte competence, rather than merely reflecting incomplete silencing. Indeed, several studies have shown that specific TE families can contribute to early embryogenesis (20, 21). For instance, full-length MERVL transcripts are required for proper regulation of the host transcriptome and chromatin organization during early embryogenesis, and repression of MERVL results in embryonic lethality due to defects in differentiation and genomic stability (20).
Together, these new analyses are presented in the revised Supplementary Fig. 10 and described in the updated Results section:
“Compared with TE subfamilies that were downregulated, these upregulated TE subfamilies showed higher transcript abundance but produced markedly fewer corresponding antisense and sense short- and long-piRNAs, accompanied by weaker Ping-Pong signatures and reduced 1U and 10A biases (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Genomic distribution analyses within the top 20 piRNA clusters further revealed substantially fewer antisense insertions for these upregulated TE subfamilies relative to downregulated TE subfamilies, consistent with their reduced antisense piRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 10b).” (Lines 333-341).
We have also added a brief discussion highlighting the potential biological relevance of increased TE subfamily expression during oocyte development:
“Notably, several TEs showed increased expression during oocyte development (Fig. 1f and Fig. 5e). Given their elevated transcript levels and the concomitant reduction in antisense piRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 10), these elements may represent evolutionarily young TEs that the PIWI-piRNA system has not yet fully adapted to silence, potentially due to insufficient antisense insertions within highly productive piRNA clusters. An alternative possibility is that their upregulation may have functional relevance for oocyte maturation. Indeed, specific TEs have been shown to play essential roles in early embryogenesis (22, 23). For example, full-length MERVL transcripts are required for proper transcriptome regulation and chromatin organization, and loss of MERVL results in embryonic lethality due to impaired differentiation and genomic instability (23). Whether the increased expression of specific TEs contributes to the acquisition of oocyte developmental competence, rather than merely reflecting incomplete silencing, therefore warrants further investigation.” (Lines 455–467).

Line 267 The Ping-Pong signature was either undetectable or 267 substantially diminished for most TE-aligned long-piRNAs. How does this vibe with other publications such as PMID: 25818294?

To evaluate whether the strength of the Ping-Pong signature observed in their dataset is consistent with ours, we reanalyzed their publicly available small RNA-seq data from adult human ovaries. Our reanalysis revealed that long-piRNAs demonstrated Ping-Pong signatures for SVA and Alu elements, whereas L1 and ERV elements exhibited very low or undetectable signals in the human ovarian samples from Roovers et al (Supplementary Figure 7). Line 364-371: It should be made clear that (control of) TE activity in germ cells is different from TE activity in somatic cells.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that TE regulation differs fundamentally between somatic and germline tissues. In somatic contexts, TE repression operates largely independently of small RNA pathways. By contrast, in germ cells, TE activity is tightly controlled by the PIWI–piRNA pathway to preserve genomic integrity and ensure proper gametogenesis.
To clarify this distinction, we have revised the Discussion section to explicitly state the difference between TE control in somatic versus germ cells, which now reads:
“In somatic cells, TE repression is maintained largely independent of small RNA pathways (24-26). By contrast, in germ cells, TE activity is tightly regulated by the PIWI-piRNA pathway, which safeguards genomic stability throughout gametogenesis (19, 27-29).” (Lines 414-417).
In addition, to avoid potential misunderstanding, we have removed the previous description suggesting ERV activity in somatic cells in the revised manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Manuscript No.: NCOMMS-25-40496 “Integrated small and long RNA sequencing in single oocytes reveals piRNA-mediated transposon repression during human oogenesis” Fengjuan Zhang, Hongdao Zhang, Yali Xiao, Miao Liu, Aimin Ren, Suying Liu2, Ligang Wu Although the piRNA pathway has been well characterized in model organisms, little is known about its functions in human gametogenesis. Large scale exome sequencing projects have identified mutations in piRNA pathway proteins that cause human male infertility, but much less is understood about piRNAs in human oocytes. In this manuscript, the authors profile the piRNAs and long RNAs in four stages of developing human oocytes. The analyses are of high quality, the data clearly presented, and the authors interpretations well supported by data and clearly described. The manuscript will be of broad interest to those studying piRNAs, gametogenesis, mammalian fertility, and TE silencing. My few concerns should be easily addressed by adding a few additional analyses and revising the text.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our study and for the constructive comments and suggestions. We have carefully addressed all points raised, adding additional analyses and revising the text accordingly to further improve the clarity and completeness of the manuscript.
Major Concerns 1.
I don’t understand the logic of these conclusions, “Collectively, these results suggest that long-piRNAs exhibit a conserved, preferential targeting of ERVs across species, indicating their specialized role in ERV repression. In contrast, short-piRNAs exhibit broader TE targeting, likely reflecting their more generalized silencing function across multiple TE families” (lines 211-214). I agree that antisense piRNAs are expected to target sense TE transcripts, but why would sense piRNAs have any function at all, other than to help amplify antisense piRNAs via the Ping-Pong cycle? Are antisense TE transcripts detected in the long RNA-seq data? Other than piRNA precursors, are there transcripts with extensive complementarity to sense piRNAs?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this question. To clarify this point, we have revised the manuscript to explicitly include strand-specific information and to distinguish the regulatory patterns of TE-related sense and antisense piRNAs. The revised text now states:
“Collectively, these results suggest that TE-related antisense long-piRNAs exhibit a conserved, preferential targeting of ERVs across species, indicating their specialized role in ERV repression. In contrast, TE-related antisense short-piRNAs exhibit broader TE targeting, likely reflecting their more generalized function across multiple TE families.” (Line 226-230)
In this study, we primarily focused on the roles of short- and long-piRNAs in TE regulation and observed distinct targeting preferences between these two piRNA populations across different TE superfamilies. However, we also recognize that the piRNA may contribute to regulatory processes beyond canonical TE silencing, particularly when TE-derived sense or antisense sequences are embedded with host protein-coding or noncoding genes. Indeed, Watanabe et al. demonstrated that in mouse spermatocytes, many mRNAs and lncRNAs harboring retrotransposon-derived sequences are repressed by the PIWIL1-piRNA pathway, and a pseudogene (Stambp-ps1) generates piRNAs that repress its parental gene (Stambp) via direct base-pairing and PIWIL1 slicer activity (30). These findings suggest that piRNAs may have broader regulatory roles beyond their canonical function in TE repression.
Because Smart-seq2 used in this study is not strand-specific, our long-RNA data cannot determine transcript orientation. Therefore, we assigned TE or gene transcript orientation based on reference annotation (TE annotation downloaded from UCSC genome browser and RepBase; gene annotation downloaded from GECODE V19). TE-related sense and antisense piRNAs were analyzed separately, and their distribution across exonic and intronic regions of different gene categories was examined (Rebuttal Figure 8). Both TE-related sense and antisense piRNAs were dispersed across multiple gene types, suggesting potential targeting activities beyond canonical TE-derived transcripts.
Within exonic regions, we observed that TE-related sense piRNAs more frequently aligned to the sense strand of protein-coding genes (>5%) compared with antisense piRNAs (~2.5%) (Rebuttal Figure 8a). Conversely, TE-related antisense piRNAs showed greater enrichment on the antisense strand of lncRNA, antisense transcripts, and pseudogenes. These observations indicate potential strand-specific regulatory interactions between piRNAs and exonic regions across diverse gene categories, mediated by the presence of TE-derived sequences.
Within intronic regions, a greater number of TE-related piRNAs were distributed across multiple gene categories and displayed distinct patterns compared with exonic regions. In addition to protein-coding genes, lincRNAs, antisense genes, and pseudogenes, TE-related piRNAs frequently aligned to intronic regions of processed transcripts and sense-overlapping loci (Rebuttal Figure 8b). Notably, TE-related sense piRNAs preferentially aligned to the antisense strand of sense-overlapping genes, whereas TE-related antisense piRNAs were more frequently associated with the sense strand of processed transcripts. These patterns raise the possibility that TE-related piRNAs may modulate RNA processing, transcript maturation, or co-transcriptional regulation through recognition of intronic TE-derived sequences.
Although these observations require further validation and the underlying mechanisms remain to be elucidated, our single-oocyte co-sequencing dataset provides a valuable resource for future studies investigating potential piRNA-mediated regulation beyond classical TE repression.

2. Was phased piRNA biogenesis detected among short or long piRNAs? Please add plots and Z-scores for the 3′ to 5′ and 5′ to 5′ distances of piRNA ends on the same genomic strand.
Response: To determine whether phased piRNAs occur in developing human oocytes, we analyzed the 3’-to-5’ and 5’-to-5’ distances between piRNA ends mapped on the same genomic strand and calculated Z-scores for phasing enrichment, following the analytical framework described by Bo W Han et al. (31). To validate our analytical pipeline, we first reanalyzed the published Tdrkh⁺/⁻ and Tdrkh⁻/⁻ mouse testis datasets, where strong phasing signatures have been reported (31, 32). Consistent with previous studies, we observed a prominent 1-nt phasing signal in the 3’-to-5’ distance distribution and broad peaks around 30-40 nt in the 5’-to-5’ distance distribution, hallmark features of phased piRNA processing (Rebuttal Figure 9a, b). Nucleotide composition analysis of downstream phased piRNA further showed a pronounced 1U bias at their 5’ ends (Rebuttal Figure 9c, d).
Rebuttal Figure 9. Phasing signatures of piRNAs in TDRKH-/- and TDRKH+/- mouse testes.
(a) Probability distribution of 3′-to-5′ distances between piRNAs mapped on the same genomic strand in Tdrkh-/- and Tdrkh+/- mouse testes. Z-scores for position 1 (phasing) are indicated.
(b) Probability distribution of 5′-to-5′ distances between piRNAs mapped on the same genomic strand in Tdrkh-/- and Tdrkh+/- mouse testes.
(c, d) Nucleotide composition of the last nucleotide of upstream piRNAs and the first nucleotide of downstream piRNAs for pairs separated by a 1-nt 3′-to-5′ distance in Tdrkh-/- (c) and Tdrkh+/- (d) mouse testes.
In developing human oocytes, the 3’-to-5’ distance analysis revealed significant enrichment at a 1-nt separation between adjacent piRNAs, with Z-scores ranging from 3.6 to 6.8 (Rebuttal Figure 10a). Short-piRNAs exhibited slightly stronger phasing signals than long-piRNAs. Nucleotide composition analysis of downstream phased piRNA showed a pronounced 1U bias at their 5’ ends, particularly among short-piRNAs (Rebuttal Figure 10c-d), consistent with canonical phased piRNA processing signatures observed in other mammals. No obvious peaks were detected in the 5′-to-5′ distance analysis (Rebuttal Figure 10b).
Interestingly, we also observed even stronger enrichment at distance = 0 than at distance = 1 (phasing) in the 3’-to-5’ distance analysis (Rebuttal Figure 10a), indicating frequent 1-nt overlaps between adjacent piRNAs. These 1-nt-overlapping downstream piRNAs similarly exhibited a strong 5′-terminal U bias, while their upstream counterparts exhibited marked enrichment for 3’-terminal U (Rebuttal Figure 10e-f). We speculate that this distinctive overlap pattern may arise from the high frequency of 3’ non-templated U tailing. However, this interpretation cannot be definitively tested with the current data, as terminal U residues cannot be reliably distinguished from tailing events. Future studies—such as perturbation of enzymes involved in piRNA 3’-end tailing—will be necessary to evaluate this model.

3. What fraction of short piRNAs were prefixes of long piRNAs (i.e., same 5′ ends)? Are the short piRNAs and long piRNAs produced from the same precursors, then trimmed to the length characteristic of the bound PIWI protein (i.e., they are prefixes) or produced by separate mechanisms?
Response: To determine whether short-piRNAs are produced from the same precursors as long-piRNAs, we analyzed the positional relationships between their 5′ and 3′ ends. Specifically, we compared the genomic coordinates of short- and long-piRNAs and calculated the probabilities that their 5′ or 3′ ends coincide. In developing human oocytes, long-piRNAs were substantially more likely to share 5′ ends with short-piRNAs than 3′ ends (0.51 vs. 0.02 in PrF; 0.68 vs. 0.01 in PF; 0.66 vs. 0.01 in GV; and 0.63 vs. 0.01 in MII). These results indicate that approximately half of long-piRNAs arise from the same 5′-cleaved precursors that generate short-piRNAs. This pattern agrees with previous findings in golden hamster MII oocytes (4) and supports a model in which short- and long-piRNAs are generated from common precursors but undergo differential 3’-end processing, likely determined by their associated PIWI proteins. Thus, the observed size differences between the two piRNA populations most likely reflect PIWI-dependent 3′-end maturation rather than distinct biogenesis pathways.
These new analyses are presented in revised Supplementary Fig. 2 and described in the corresponding Results section (Line 181-185) of the revised manuscript, which reads as:
“Genomic coordinate analysis showed that short- and long-piRNAs were far more likely to share 5’ ends than 3’ ends across all stages (PrF: 0.51 vs. 0.02; PF: 0.68 vs. 0.01; GV: 0.66 vs. 0.01; MII: 0.63 vs. 0.01) (Supplementary Fig. 2), suggesting that both populations are derived from the same 5’-cleaved precursors, consistent with findings in golden hamster (4).”

8. Throughout the text, please clarify whether the piRNA or long RNA data being discussed is restricted to uniquely mapping reads or includes multiply mapping reads, and, if it includes multi-mappers, whether they were apportioned among all loci or randomly assigned to individual loci.
Response: For multiply mapped piRNAs or long reads, each read was assigned to all possible mapped loci and categorized by TE superfamily in the following order: LINE/L1 → SINE/Alu → LTR/ERV → LTR/others → SVA → others. Because individual TE subfamilies (e.g., L1PA1 and L1PA2) share high sequence similarity, we applied a greedy mapping strategy to capture all potential alignments. If a read or piRNA species mapped to multiple TE subfamilies within the same superfamily, it was counted in each subfamily. However, when summarizing results at the superfamily level (e.g., LINE/L1), each piRNA or read was counted only once. For instance, a piRNA mapping to both L1PA1 and L1PA2 was counted once in the LINE-1 superfamily summary but included in both subfamilies when L1PA1- and L1PA2-derived piRNAs were analyzed separately. This strategy was applied consistently across all TE-related analyses, including TE transcript level, TE-associated short- and long-piRNAs, and strand-specific subsets, to ensure uniform quantification and accurate cross-dataset comparison.
We have carefully revised the text to clarify which long RNA reads or piRNA categories (uniquely mapped, multiply mapped, or both) were used in each analysis and have explicitly specified these details in the Materials and Methods section (Lines 565-573) and relevant figure legends.
